experiments.title: EURISKO literature study

page.why: We wanted to know whether EURISKO's old idea, rules of thumb that rewrite other rules of thumb, has anything left for modern AI search.
page.what: A research workflow read the EURISKO papers and critics, Yudkowsky's early writing, the Bend2 language, and recent LLM-plus-scorer systems; two judges scored three experiment designs.
page.result: LLM-plus-scorer loops find real wins; nobody has shown rules rewriting rules beats plain evolution at equal compute.
page.sowhat: The idea is untested rather than refuted. Bend2 was not ready to be the engine for program search.
page.decided: We did not fund the proposed 2-week, ~$650 algorithm-speed run and turned to self-modifying agents and markets of traders instead.

methods: A research workflow read EURISKO's papers, its critics and the recovered 1981 source, Yudkowsky's early writing, Bend2's docs and code, and recent LLM-plus-scorer systems.
Every quoted claim was fetched on 27 Sep 2026; two critic passes then revised the report. Unfetched claims are marked unverified.
Three experiment designs were written; two judges scored each; critics checked the winner.
The winning design (WTO-AlgoTune: LLM-written search heuristics with tracked Worth, 10 AlgoTune tasks, 6 train and 4 held out) was costed at ~$650, cap $900, two weeks.
No numbers reported: literature study, no experiment ran; the table shows design scores only.

experiments.title: Self-modifying agents (DGM) reading

page.why: After [[eurisko-literature-study|the EURISKO study]], we wanted to see whether self-modifying coding agents such as the Darwin Gödel Machine could run far faster on Bend2.
page.what: A research workflow read the DGM line of papers and code, traced where the compute goes, and ranked Bend-friendly self-modifier ideas.
page.result: DGM's cost is almost all LLM runs (~$22k per run, SWE-bench score 20→50%); selection code is about 50 lines.
page.sowhat: Bend2 cannot speed up LLM calls. It only helps when each evaluation is a tiny symbolic program.
page.decided: Paper only: no DGM experiment ran, and we moved to a market of tiny trader programs instead.

experiments.title: Soup: traders per question

page.why: Logical induction says a market of many traders ends up with good, consistent probabilities. We wanted to see how far [[eurisko-literature-study|evolving trader programs]] get on their own.
page.what: One Bend2 program held 4k to 64k tiny trader programs betting in an automated market on up to 4096 synthetic yes/no sequences. Rich traders reproduced and broke ones died. We varied traders and questions, 3 seeds, 5000 epochs.

chart.caption: Brier on periodic sequences (lower is better; always 50% scores 0.25)
chart.aria: Brier falls from 0.241 to 0.084 as traders per question rise

page.result: What matters is traders per question. At 16 per question, 4k, 16k and 64k traders all score the same (≈0.13). More per question kept helping up to 64, the highest we tried (0.084); above that is untested.
page.sowhat: At 64 traders per question the market prices easy patterns and beats simple reference traders. The lever is population density, not size.
page.decided: We tested the other obvious lever, compute per trader, next.

methods: One Bend2 program: 4k–64k trader programs (tiny stack machines, 256 instructions per run) trade in an LMSR market on 256–4096 synthetic yes/no questions.
Question families: periodic, primality, LFSR, cellular automata 30 and 110, pi digits, plus A∧B and A∨B compounds.
Wealth is the only currency and the market maker's subsidy the only inflow; rich traders split, poor ones die. The ledger balances exactly every epoch.
7 cells (K traders × Q questions), 3 seeds each, 5000 epochs. Score: Brier, mean of the last 50 epochs; always-50% scores 0.25.
Ran on the JS lane here and on spot L4 GPUs (64k cells); GPU spend $9.38.

experiments.title: Soup: consistency arbitrageur

page.why: In logical induction a trader that exploits inconsistent prices forces the market to be consistent. We wanted to see if such a trader evolves by itself [[soup-traders-per-question|in our soup]].
page.what: We ran a fixed arbitrage trader on paper beside the market, tracking its profit and how far P(A and B) rose above P(A) or P(B).

chart.caption: Brier at 64 traders per question (lower is better)
chart.aria: A and B priced, A or B not

page.result: The arbitrageur profited in every setting; P(A and B) stayed 0.01–0.09 too high.
page.sowhat: The market priced “A and B” but not “A or B”. The trader that enforces consistency never evolved.
page.decided: We turned to Jessica's question: can the traders live inside one neural network instead?

methods: Same 7 soup cells (1–64 traders per question, 3 seeds, 5000 epochs).
A fixed coherence arbitrageur ran in a shadow ledger: it trades against the prices but never moves them or replicates.
Profit: slope of its cumulative profit over the last 1000 epochs, in shares per epoch; positive means the market leaves money on the table.
AND violation: max(0, P(A∧B) − min(P(A), P(B))).
Score: Brier, mean of the last 50 epochs over 3 seeds.

experiments.title: Soup on GPU (Bend2)

page.why: Bend2 promises to run one program in parallel on a GPU. We wanted to know if that makes [[soup-traders-per-question|the soup]] much bigger or faster.
page.what: We ran the same soup on the JavaScript lane, native CPU and CUDA on L4 and A100 GPUs, checked the outputs were byte-identical, and profiled where time goes.

experiments.title: Why traders per question matters

page.why: We wanted a simple explanation for why [[soup-traders-per-question|traders per question]], and not total traders, sets the score.
page.what: We fit a lottery model: each trader per question is one more ticket for finding the pattern. We then varied traders per question inside a neural-network version.
page.result: The lottery model fits the soup with R² 0.79–0.94; in the network, 1 to 64 traders per question shows no trend.
page.sowhat: The law is about search by random programs, not about markets.
page.decided: Recorded as a finding; no follow-up run.

methods: Data: the 21 soup runs (7 cells × 3 seeds, mean of the last 50 of 5000 epochs).
Model: Brier = 0.25 − D·(1 − (1 − π)^(K/Q)); each trader per question is a ticket that finds the pattern with chance π.
Compared with log-linear and saturating curves by AIC; null: K/Q labels shuffled 1000 times. π CIs by bootstrap.
Network test: 64 synthetic questions, a small transformer trunk with 1–64 trader heads per question, 2 arms × 2 series × 3 seeds (42 runs); score: BCE on learnable families.
CPU only; reruns were byte-identical.

experiments.title: Trader economy with niches

page.why: Evolving markets tend to end with one winner owning everything. We checked what keeps many kinds of traders alive.
page.what: Simulated trader species with and without niches (one question per trader), against a shuffled-beliefs control.

chart.caption: Wealth Gini (lower is more equal)
chart.aria: Gini 0.44 with niches vs 0.74 null

page.result: Without niches one species holds ≥99.7% of the wealth; with niches every slot survives and the market reaches the best possible Brier.
page.sowhat: Diversity needs niches. Charging for compute only destroyed wealth.
page.decided: Recorded as a finding; no follow-up run.

methods: Kelly bettors in a pari-mutuel pool; species = kind (pattern-k counts or online logistic) × k.
Price = stake-weighted mean belief; a maker adds 1% of initial wealth per step; traders split at wealth 4 and die below 0.01.
Niches on: each trader trades one question. Control: the same population with shuffled beliefs, on the same stream.
1k, 10k and 100k traders, 64 or 4096 questions, 10,000 steps, 3 seeds; CPU only. Money conserved to 4.1e-12 in all 141 runs.
Score: tail Brier against the oracle; inequality: wealth Gini.

tables.note: ± = sd over 3 seeds. Niches off, Q64: top species holds 0.9969 ± 0.0046 of wealth. Source: traders-net study, K1.

experiments.title: Wealth books on a small network

page.why: After [[soup-arbitrageur|the soup's consistency trader never evolved]], with Jessica we asked whether the units of a neural network can act as traders, each earning from how much it helps. First test: pay each neuron its backprop credit and see if the poorest are useless.
page.what: A 2-layer transformer with 512 neurons learned the soup's sequences, 3 seeds. Each step, every neuron was paid its gradient credit. We then deleted the poorest neurons and compared with random and smallest-gradient deletions on fresh data.

chart.caption: Fresh-data loss (lower is better)
chart.aria: Removing poorest neurons hurts most

page.result: The poorest neurons are load-bearing: deleting 1% raises loss 0.25; deleting random 1% raises it 0.02.
page.sowhat: Backprop credit, summed as wealth, points the wrong way on the neurons that matter.
page.decided: We tried other currencies: recent income, then exact payment.

methods: 64 questions in 8 families from the logical soup (periodic, LFSR-16, CA rules 30 and 110, primality, pi-digit parity, A and B, A or B); 24,000 steps of stream per seed, trained on the first 80%.
Model: 2-layer transformer, 512 MLP neurons, 8 heads; Adam 1e-3, batch 128; 3 seeds, about 31k steps each (50-minute cap).
Books: every step each neuron was paid its gradient credit (input times gradient), summed as wealth.

Test: delete 1-40% of neurons by five rules (poorest, poorest recent, random as the mean of 5 draws, smallest gradient, smallest activation) and score loss (BCE) on positions 24,000-28,095, never seen in training. Mean of 3 seeds, no intervals.
Cost: about $1.02 of spot L4 GPU (list-price ceiling).

experiments.title: Recent income as wealth

page.why: [[wealth-books|All-time wealth]] is history. Maybe recent income is the currency that matters.
page.what: We turned each neuron's income into decayed wealth with half-lives of 100 to 10,000 steps and compared with the true effect of removing each neuron.

chart.caption: Rank correlation with each neuron's true value (higher is better)
chart.aria: No currency tracks true value

page.result: No recent-income measure tracks true value; all correlations sit within ±0.11 of zero.
page.sowhat: Wealth singles out the important neurons but ranks them at either extreme, so its sign is unreliable.
page.decided: We replaced gradient credit with the market's own payment.

experiments.title: Exact payment (leave-one-out)

page.why: [[wealth-books|Backprop credit]] and [[decayed-wealth|recent income]] failed. A market pays a trader what its bet actually gained. We tested paying each neuron the real log-score gain it causes at the output.
page.what: Three payments: leave-one-out gain, a layer-by-layer split, and sampled Shapley. Each was summed on training data and ranked against the true removal effect.

chart.caption: Rank correlation with true neuron value, training data (higher is better)
chart.aria: Leave-one-out best

page.result: Leave-one-out payment tracks true value (+0.42 ± 0.03; +0.58 on held-out) and is the best pruning rule tested.
page.sowhat: Paying for real gain works as wealth; summing gradients does not. Shapley, the “fair” split, was useless.
page.decided: Wealth must be a settled payout, never a running sum of gradients.

methods: Same 3 trained networks; CPU only, no training, 10 minutes.

Each neuron's direct push on the output logit (matches a real removal to 7e-6) was priced three ways: leave-one-out log-score gain, a layer-by-layer split, and sampled Shapley (8 random orders per example).
Summed over 4,096 training positions (what a market would see) and over the held-out segment (an upper bound: same labels as the oracle).
Score: Spearman rank correlation with the single-neuron removal effect, per seed; the traders-net study reran it (mean ± sd, fresh held-out segment).

experiments.title: Backprop credit vs payout

page.why: We wanted to measure how often [[wealth-books|backprop credit]] and [[exact-settlement|a market payout]] disagree in sign, on the neurons that matter most.
page.what: The traders-net study (3 seeds) counted, among the 5% most important neurons, how many look bankrupt under each currency. A toy model proved why.

chart.caption: Share of the top 5% neurons with negative wealth (lower is better)

page.result: A quarter of the key neurons look bankrupt under backprop credit, against 3% under exact payment.
page.sowhat: Once training settles, a useful unit earns zero or negative gradient credit, yet removing it hurts. This is the core problem.
page.decided: Ordinary neurons get no running wealth: a trader must commit to a price on a defined question and be paid when it resolves.

experiments.title: Block-local payment

page.why: Building on [[exact-settlement|exact payment]]: if each block of the network is paid for its own prediction, its payment might match its real value.
page.what: Each block trained on its own loss with no gradient crossing block boundaries, 3 seeds. We also let a share of the gradient leak across.

chart.caption: Rank correlation of payment with true unit value (higher is better)
chart.aria: Block-local payment tracks value

page.result: Block-local payment tracks true value at +0.86 against +0.40 end-to-end, and held-out loss fell 1.042 → 0.859.
page.sowhat: Paying each block for its own prediction makes payment honest. The loss gain is less memorisation of unpredictable questions, not better learning. 3 seeds, not rechecked.
page.decided: We added a market on top of the blocks.

experiments.title: Trader heads and market layers

page.why: [[sign-census|Backprop credit often got the sign wrong]]. If a trader must commit to a price, we can give the network heads that each commit a correction and get paid.
page.what: The traders-net study tested market-layer designs and committed trader heads against plain layers, 3 seeds; ten designs were not clearly worse.
page.result: Kept market layers win only 0.001 on noise questions; committed heads lower loss 0.3–1.3%, but their wealth does not track their value (correlation −0.002).
page.sowhat: Small gains, and the wealth inside does not mean anything yet.
page.decided: No follow-up run.

True value: loss increase on the last 25% when one trader is removed; wealth summed on the first 75%.
Market layers: 15 designs; drop rule: 1% or more worse than the plain layer in 3/3 seeds and no extra protection on noise questions.

page.why: Mixture-of-experts routing already balances load with a price. We asked whether expert wealth routes better.

experiments.title: Is the network consistent before answers arrive?

page.why: A logical inductor is consistent before questions resolve. We checked the network's own probabilities.
page.what: We measured how often the network's prices break logical rules (for example P(A and B) above P(A)) over 3 seeds, and ran an online probe that tries to exploit them.

chart.caption: Violation rate (lower is better)
chart.aria: Violation rates near 0.5

page.result: Violation rates match an uninformed market's, and a test trader profited on every fresh run.
page.sowhat: Training on outcomes alone does not make the network consistent.
page.decided: Recorded; the exploit sizes did not reproduce, so we report only the violation rates.

experiments.title: Wealth lock-in after a shift

page.why: Rich traders can stay rich after the world changes. We tested which wealth rule recovers.

experiments.title: Regulator pays by counterfactuals

experiments.title: Market ResNet: liquidity that grows with depth

page.why: Past the training length the [[depth-mresnet-phase2|economy’s beliefs run away]]. We tested a bound with a market reading: liquidity that grows with each step, so late trades move prices less.

experiments.title: Private memory slots priced online

experiments.title: Capping how far each step moves the belief

page.why: A market bounds each trade by its worst-case loss. We tested whether that cap keeps a maze net stable when it runs far longer than in training.

experiments.title: Paying hidden variables bits saved minus bits to learn

page.why: [[depth-p3-latent-codes|Shapley-type pay]] did not find good hidden variables. We tested a price that pays a hidden variable for the output bits it saves minus the bits it costs to learn.

experiments.title: A fast reader prices hidden variables

page.why: In [[puzzle-p8-bits-price|the bits-to-learn price test]] only a costly wrapper ranked intermediates well. We tested whether a cheap fast reader's gain ranks them as well.
page.what: A warm-start copy of the current reader gets each candidate as a new input and trains for 64 short chunks; its prequential gain is the price. 44 maze items, 5 seeds, against a first-order price, importance alone and P8's wrapper. Pre-registered kill rules.
page.result: Killed: it ranks at tau 0.576, below the 0.70 kill line, and beats the first-order price by only 0.046 (the margin was 0.05). P8's wrapper reaches 0.87.
page.sowhat: Cheap pricing of this kind does not rank intermediates well. Only the wrapper, which deploys a predicted intermediate, prices XOR-type candidates correctly.
page.decided: Stop this fast reader. Untested: a cheap price on the predicted rather than the true intermediate.

experiments.title: Price correction inside a maze solver

page.why: [[depth-p11-belief-caps|Capping each step]] did not help a maze solver think longer. We tested a trader that corrects the solver’s edge prices with exact flow checks inside the loop.
page.what: Weighted mazes, trained at 9×9 and tested 3–7× wider. After each step, belief propagation over flow constraints corrected the recurrent solver’s edge prices (no gradient through it). experiments.title: Buying restarts or depth per Sudoku

page.why: In [[depth-costnet-bb|the learned-costs test]] an exact solver did the work, and [[puzzle-p14-listing|value-priced listing]] lost to plain baselines. We tested a market that buys compute for a known Sudoku solver, paid on a check anyone can run.
page.what: The released EqR Sudoku-Extreme solver (Huang, Geng and Kolter 2026). Traders price each next restart or 2× more depth per puzzle, at equal compute with the paper's selection rules. Pre-registered, 2,048 test puzzles.
page.result: The market scores 98.54% at 64 steps per puzzle, beating smallest residual (92.72%) and majority vote (92.38%), but restart-until-valid scores 98.49%, a tie.
page.sowhat: The gain comes from the validity check and a shared budget, not from pricing. The market learned to restart rather than deepen, which a fixed rule already does.
page.decided: No maze follow-up: the pre-registered secondary test failed.

chart.caption: Exact on 2,048 test puzzles at 64 steps per puzzle (equal compute); market − restart-until-valid +0.05 [0.00, +0.15] points
chart.aria: Market and restart-until-valid tie, both far above the paper's selection rules

methods: Bank: 128 restarts × a staircase of depths per puzzle (8,192 steps); every policy is replayed from it with exact per-puzzle step counts. One step is one outer EqR step.
Market actions: start a restart or extend a candidate 2×. Settlement is the Sudoku constraint check; no labels are used at run time, and no test grid is valid but wrong.

Kill rule (beat smallest residual and majority vote) passed: +5.81 [+4.83, +6.84] and +6.15 [+5.13, +7.23] points. Secondary test (beat restart-until-valid) failed: +0.05 [0.00, +0.15], 1 puzzle won and 0 lost.
At 64 steps the market made 8,519 restarts and 626 extensions; the extensions used 13% of the steps and produced 1 valid grid.
With a fixed budget per puzzle (no pooling), the market's choices equal restart-until-valid on every puzzle (93.41%); pooling the budget across puzzles adds the other 5.1 points.
Amendment 1: path noise 0.5 failed gate G1 (76.07%), so noise was set to 0.01, the paper's single-restart setting, before any market or test data. It reproduces the paper's Table 4 (86.4 and 93.0).
An independent verifier passed all 9 checks. Cost $10.76 (12 spot L4 VMs, 7 preemptions).

experiments.title: Consistency on real short-horizon questions (MiniBench backtest, 347 questions)

page.why: [[make-answers-consistent|Making answers consistent]] helped on our own question sets, but a 30-question MiniBench dry run showed no gain (C − B +0.2 [−2.0, +2.6]). We rechecked on 347 real Metaculus questions that resolve within about two weeks.
page.what: Opus 5.5 forecast every scorable question from six MiniBench rounds that opened after its training cutoff, as of each question's open time, with research cut there. Arm B is plain; arm C adds the consistency projection. Pre-registered; nothing was submitted.
page.result: No gain: C − B = −0.30 [−1.92, +1.41] Metaculus baseline points; on binary questions −0.44 [−1.43, +0.61]. After fixing a blend bug in arm C: +0.69 (Opus), +0.82 (Luna), not significant; exploratory.
page.sowhat: Plain forecasts are good (B beats uniform by +31.3 and the bot crowd by +4.2), but consistency adds nothing on these single-event questions: on binary ones C equals the P / NOT-P average 89% of the time.
page.decided: Keep plain B as the arm to submit.

chart.aria: Plain and consistent forecasts tie

methods: Sample: 348 resolved questions from rounds 33064–33122 (opened 29 Jun to 7 Sep 2026); 318 forecast fresh and 30 reused from the dry run with the same code. The leak audit dropped 1, so n = 347: 178 binary, 80 discrete, 76 numeric, 13 multiple choice.
Every forecast on claude-opus-5-5; research from 4 Exa searches cut at the as-of time; hash-chained ledgers verify.

Primary: paired C − B in Metaculus baseline points, 10,000-resample bootstrap. The planned minimum detectable effect was 1.1 points; the observed SD was 2.2× the plan, so the pre-registered sub-label is inconclusive rather than 'gain ruled out'. A gain above +0.6 on binary questions is excluded.
Leak audit of 20 random questions: 1 had confirmed post-cutoff text (a page updated after the cutoff without changing its date) and was dropped. The Problem bar was 2.

A scorer edge case on two numeric questions (outcomes exactly on a CDF grid edge) was fixed and everything rescored from the saved forecasts; the headline moved from −0.27 [−1.89, +1.45] to −0.30 [−1.92, +1.41], and an independent rescoring matches.

Exploratory, after the Luna follow-up: a blend bug in arm C emptied buckets that B gave real mass (57 of Opus's 156 numeric and discrete questions). It was fixed and C rescored from the saved answers with no new model calls: C′ − B +0.69 [−0.45, +2.14]. B stays the submit arm.
Cost $101.69 (forecasts $100.70, audit $0.99).

experiments.title: Detached per-step training on mazes

page.why: The [[depth-mresnet-order|Market ResNet audit]] left one survivor: detached per-step training in random order. On prefix sums [[depth-mresnet-dtrecall|DT-Recall still beat it]]. We tested it on mazes against DT-Recall, the [[depth-p0-baseline|baseline]] for these puzzles.
page.what: Four untied recurrent blocks, each step trained on its own loss from a detached state, block drawn in random order (A1), against DT-Recall with the progressive loss (Bansal et al. 2022). Trained on 9×9 mazes, tested up to 59×59, at equal compute. Pre-registered.
page.result: No gain (the pre-registered kill fired): A1 solves 0.017 of 59×59 mazes, DT-Recall 0.081; A1 − DT-Recall −0.064 [−0.111, −0.017].
page.sowhat: A1's four blocks fall into a period-4 cycle on 69% of 59×59 mazes; DT-Recall's shared block cycles on 2.5%. Random order helps at 19×19 (+0.25) but not at 59×59.
page.decided: Detached random-order training is dropped for mazes; DT-Recall with the progressive loss stays the bar.

chart.caption: Exact on 200 test 59×59 mazes at 12n steps, equal compute, seed means; A1 − DT-Recall −0.064 [−0.111, −0.017]
chart.aria: DT-Recall beats detached random-order training on large mazes

methods: Arms, width 128, trained on official 9×9 mazes with the official recipe (no gradient clipping): A1 four untied DT-Recall blocks, detached per-step loss, random block order; A2 the same in round-robin order; A3 the same with full backprop through depth; A4 DT-Recall with the progressive loss at α = 0, 0.5 and 1, with α = 1 picked on dev 59×59 mazes.
Equal compute: 1.7 L4-hours of training per run (realised 1.67–1.78 h). DT-Recall α = 1 still got about 13% more counted FLOPs and 2.7× the optimizer steps.

Metric: exact maze accuracy at T = 12n on held-out test sets of 200 (19×19), 300 (33×33) and 200 (59×59) mazes. Primary: Welch one-sided test, 5 seeds against 5, one-sided 95% bounds; kill if the upper bound is below 0. It fired; a Mann-Whitney test gives p = 0.016.
Detachment helps training, not reach: full backprop through four untied blocks trained on 0/3 seeds in 1.7 h. DT-Recall at α = 0 and 0.5 was unstable without clipping (1/3 and 0/3 seeds trained).

DT-Recall α = 1 also trains from detached states. The gap is one shared block with random-length gradient windows against four untied blocks with one-step windows; the one-block arm that would separate these was not run (spend rule).
The budget is about 36–40% of the official recipe, which reaches 0.915 on 59×59. Other test-time block orders were not tested.
Pre-registered; an independent verifier agrees. Cost $36.40 of a $40 cap (61 spot L4 VMs, all deleted).

experiments.title: Does the consistency gain shrink for stronger models?

page.why: [[make-answers-consistent|Making answers consistent]] cut log loss for the Qwen models, but in the [[minibench-backtest-347|MiniBench backtest]] Opus 5.5 gained nothing. We asked whether stronger models gain less, on the same pairs.
page.what: Four models answer the same 300 test pairs, 12 forms each, one form per call, same wording: Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B (existing answers), GPT-6 Luna without reasoning and Opus 5.5 at low effort. Gain = log loss after the projection minus before. Pre-registered.
page.result: Informative: gain in log loss 32B −0.074, 235B −0.036, Luna −0.071, Opus 5.5 −0.005. It follows how inconsistent each model is (P vs NOT-P correlation −0.54, −0.77, −0.80, −0.98), not strength alone: Luna is about as accurate as 235B and gains twice as much.
page.sowhat: Opus 5.5 is already nearly consistent, so there is little to fix; this explains the MiniBench null. Its raw 0.368 may partly be recall of outcomes from before its cutoff, but on the 127 pairs it is unsure about it still gains only −0.005, while the other models gain −0.038 to −0.078 there.
page.decided: Projection is for inconsistent answerers (small models, frontier models without reasoning), not for Opus 5.5.

chart.caption: Log-loss gain from making answers consistent, same 300 pairs (longer bar = more gain); P vs NOT-P correlation −0.54, −0.77, −0.80, −0.98
chart.aria: 32B and Luna gain most, 235B less, Opus 5.5 almost nothing

methods: Pairs: the 300 test pairs of the structure-vs-averaging run (Manifold pair test set), 12 stated forms each, one form per call, with the clear NOT wording; no search or tools.

Models: Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B at temperature 0 without thinking (existing answers); GPT-6 Luna at reasoning effort none and Opus 5.5 at effort low, both at the provider's default temperature (their routes take no temperature). The served model was checked on every call; no arm stopped or was substituted.

Gain: all-12 log loss after the kl coherence projection minus before, probabilities clipped to [0.01, 0.99]; negative helps. 95% paired bootstrap over pairs, 2,000 resamples. Bars: No gain if the CI lower bound is at least −0.01, Gain if the CI upper bound is below 0.

Opus 5.5 is No gain by that bar (−0.005 [−0.008, −0.003]: nonzero but under 0.01); Luna is Gain. Against 235B, Opus is much stronger (raw −0.180 [−0.211, −0.148]) and gains less (+0.031 [+0.025, +0.036]), so the pre-registered reading is 'shrinks'. Luna is not significantly stronger than 235B (−0.018 [−0.048, +0.013]) and gains more (−0.035 [−0.049, −0.021]).

Recall: the test questions closed May–Dec 2025, before Opus 5.5's training cutoff. 34% of its single-event answers are at most 0.05 or at least 0.95, and 98.5% of those are right, so the pre-registered recall flag is on. The unsure-pairs check (label-free: pairs where the model's own P and Q are both in [0.10, 0.90]) shows the small gain is not only recall.
Limits: the frontier models ran at default temperature and one effort level each.

Pre-registered before any Luna or Opus call; all 300 pairs complete for all four models, 0 missing forms. An independent verifier recomputed 150 numbers from the raw logs (largest difference 1.7e-9). Cost $31.00 of a $60 cap.

experiments.title: DT-Recall: the official recipe, 3 seeds

page.why: [[depth-p0-baseline|DT-Recall]] is the bar for our depth tests, but on mazes our own short runs sat far below the paper, in [[depth-p18-detached-mazes|P18]] and next to [[depth-costnet-bb|learned costs]]. We reproduced the official code, configs and data, 3 seeds per task.
page.what: The official deep-thinking code (Schwarzschild et al. 2021, Bansal et al. 2022), unmodified, with the paper's configs and data, trained 3 times per task and scored on the paper's test sets, our P13 mazes and the Market ResNet strings. The authors' released checkpoints were scored the same way.
page.result: Informative: prefix sums reproduce (512-bit 98.97, 100, 100% vs the paper's 97.12). Mazes vary hugely by seed: 59×59 9.1, 99.8, 87.2% (paper 97.3, released checkpoint 100); 201×201, first 20 mazes, 0, 35, 0% (paper 74 of 100, released 46).
page.sowhat: Our own maze baselines were far weaker than the released model: on the same 59×59 mazes P18's DT-Recall solved 8.1% and P13's 31%, the released checkpoint 99.5%. Maze comparisons should use the released checkpoint.
page.decided: Compare maze results against the released checkpoint (or maze seed 1), not our own short runs.

chart.caption: Exact on 1,000 test 59×59 mazes, best over test-time steps; paper 97.30 ± 0.68
chart.aria: One of three seeds matches the paper on large mazes; the released checkpoint scores 100%

methods: Official deep-thinking code at a pinned commit, unmodified; easy-to-hard data tarballs checked by sha256. Training adds only seeding, strict FP32 and exact resume after spot preemption. One L4 per run.
Prefix sums: width 400, progressive loss α = 1, trained on 32-bit strings, 150 epochs. Mazes: width 128, α = 0.01, trained on 9×9, 50 epochs, about 7.1 L4-hours per seed.
Scored: exact accuracy at every test-time step, peak reported, plus accuracy at the paper's step count. Our evaluator matches the official forward bitwise on every model.

All seeds pass the paper's convergence filter (training accuracy ≥ 99%). Maze training collapses and recovers several times, also in the released run's own log, and the checkpoint is picked on 9×9 validation, which says nothing about how far a seed extrapolates.
Market ResNet prefix strings: every trained model and the released one solve 100% at L32, L320 and L3200 given about L/3 steps (seed 0: 93% on one L3200 set).
Cost about $20.85 of a $25 cap (19 spot L4 VMs, all deleted).

experiments.title: Consistency on MiniBench with Luna

page.why: [[consistency-strength-scaling|On the same pairs]] GPT-6 Luna gained as much from consistency as 32B, while Opus 5.5 gained almost nothing, which explained the [[minibench-backtest-347|MiniBench null]]. We replayed the MiniBench backtest with Luna to see whether its gain shows up on real questions.
page.what: The same 347 questions, evidence, prompts and arms as the Opus backtest; only the forecast calls switch to Luna without reasoning. Arm B is plain; arm C adds the consistency step. Pre-registered; nothing was submitted.
page.result: No gain (pre-registered sub-label: C worse): C − B = −6.36 [−11.63, −1.56] Metaculus baseline points. Luna C − Opus B = −18.07 [−24.44, −11.98]. After fixing a blend bug in arm C: +0.69 (Opus), +0.82 (Luna), not significant; exploratory.
page.sowhat: The loss came from discrete questions (C − B −22.85), all from a blend bug in arm C's numeric step, now fixed: with the fix C no longer loses, but it does not significantly gain either. On binary questions, where the pair result predicted a gain, C − B is +0.81 [−1.68, +3.43], not significant. Against the bot crowd: Opus B +4.18, Opus C +3.86, Luna B −7.31, Luna C −6.80.
page.decided: Keep plain Opus B; a gain from the fixed C would need its own pre-registered test on new questions.

chart.caption: Mean Metaculus baseline score per question, 347 questions, pre-registered (before the blend fix); Luna C − B −6.36 [−11.63, −1.56]
chart.aria: Opus beats Luna, and consistency lowers Luna's score

methods: Replay of the MiniBench backtest: same 347 questions (178 binary, 80 discrete, 76 numeric, 13 multiple choice), stored evidence, Opus planner output, prompts, forms, arms and fixed scorer. Only the form calls change model: GPT-6 Luna at reasoning effort none, provider-default sampling, no search. Opus ran at medium effort, so Luna vs Opus compares a fast model without reasoning with a frontier model with it.
Primary: paired Luna C − B in Metaculus baseline points, 10,000-resample bootstrap; pre-registered before any Luna call. No Problem check fired: every call served Luna, 1 of 1,900 forms unparsed.

Why C loses (exploratory): on numeric and discrete questions arm C blends the threshold answers into B's distribution. Where they disagree, pooling empties buckets that B gave real mass, and an outcome there scores about −225. Luna has such a bucket on 34 of 80 discrete questions (Opus 20). Without discrete questions Luna C − B is −1.41 [−5.96, +2.76]. The fix rescales B's distribution between thresholds instead; emptied buckets fall from 95 to 0 (Luna) and 57 to 0 (Opus) of 156, and a regression test covers it.

Coherence on binary questions: Luna's P vs NOT-P correlation −0.891, Opus −0.989. Luna is less consistent, but MiniBench's binary chain has fewer forms than the 12 per pair, and the gain there is +0.81, not significant.

Training cutoffs: Luna 2026-05-18, Opus June 2026. Every question opened on or after 29 Jun 2026; all resolved after Luna's cutoff (42 to 125 days) and all but one after Opus's. Recall check (Opus − Luna in Jun–Jul minus Aug–Sep): +7.97 [−2.73, +19.15], so no sign that Opus relies on remembered outcomes, though a few points are not ruled out.
An independent verifier matched all 11 checks. Cost $1.10 (1,901 Luna calls).

experiments.title: Market ResNet on mazes

page.why: [[depth-mresnet-caps|Capping runaway beliefs]] fixed the Market ResNet on prefix parity, where [[depth-mresnet-dtrecall|DT-Recall still beat it]]. We ported it to mazes: train on 9×9, test at 99×99, against DT-Recall at equal compute. [[depth-p18-detached-mazes|P18]] tested detached per-step training on the same mazes.
page.what: Market ResNet with belief logits capped at 10, trained on 9×9 mazes only, against DT-Recall retrained at the same 3.0 L4-hours; the same economy with the wealth cap off; the released DT-Recall checkpoint as a reference. 4 seeds per trained arm. Pre-registered.
page.result: No gain (the pre-registered falsifier F1 holds): every Market ResNet model solves 0.00 of 99×99 mazes; DT-Recall at equal compute 0.21 (seeds 0 / 0.83 / 0 / 0), the released model 0.94.

experiments.title: Weekly world model: fixing the overrated “A and B”

page.why: In the [[and-only-world-model-35-weeks|“And”-only world model]], multiplying single answers beat every fitted joint, because stated “A and B” sits about 0.07 above that product. We tried two fixes on the six sampled weeks: a prompt that warns about the bias, and thinking mode.
page.what: Qwen3-32B on the “A and B” and “A and B and C” questions of six sampled weeks. Correction prompt: the base prompt plus one warning paragraph, 6,000 joints. Thinking mode: 262 joints plus their 558 single questions. Baseline: the product of the base run's single answers. Comparisons pre-registered. A held-out check reran the frozen prompt on 6,000 joints from the train split.
page.result: Informative: the correction prompt beats the product of singles on joint log loss by −0.046 [−0.058, −0.035] over 6,000 joints; held-out check on 6,000 unseen train-split joints: −0.062 [−0.078, −0.046]; same months (no newer weeks exist). On Manifold pairs (all four joint forms) it does not transfer: joint − product-of-singles +0.016 [+0.001, +0.032]. It helps P∧Q (−0.025) but hurts ¬P∧¬Q (+0.148); projection of corrected answers is slightly worse (+0.0055). Thinking beats it by −0.024 [−0.045, −0.002] over 262 joints and improves the singles by 0.11 nats.
page.sowhat: The prompt was designed from the bias in the test weeks and still wins on held-out events, where the bias itself replicates (base prompt − product +0.046 [+0.027, +0.064]). The held-out events come from the same months, so a later period is untested. The gain holds only for AND-of-positives, the form the weekly model uses: the paragraph pushes every AND answer down, which is wrong for ¬P∧¬Q, true in 47.5% of Manifold pairs. The prompt costs about 1/25 of thinking per call. Thinking helps joints through better singles: the product of its own singles (0.161) beats its stated joints (0.203).
page.decided: The paragraph fits AND-of-positives questions like the weekly model's, not joint questions in general; a later-period check needs newer weeks and a new Luna graph.

chart.caption: Joint outcome log loss on 6,000 joints, lower is better; correction − product −0.046 [−0.058, −0.035]; held-out check −0.062 [−0.078, −0.046]
chart.aria: The correction prompt has the lowest joint log loss

methods: Qwen3-32B on the 17,531 resolved “A and B” and “A and B and C” questions of the six sampled weeks, in one seeded random order; each arm takes a prefix.

Correction prompt: the base joint prompt plus one paragraph saying such statements are rated too high, cannot be more likely than the least likely question, and are usually near the product of the separate probabilities. Thinking off, temperature 0, the first 6,000 joints; singles not re-asked.

Thinking mode: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, thinking budget 4,000 tokens; the first 262 joints plus the single question of every event in them. The count came from a $14 spend rule fixed before any outcome was read.

Baseline: the product of the base run's single answers, same week. Outcome log loss clipped to [0.01, 0.99], paired, with a 95% event-cluster bootstrap CI (2,000 resamples) and a week-block CI alongside. The comparisons and decision rule were written before any arm call.

The correction paragraph was written from the bias seen in these same weeks. Held-out check, pre-registered: the byte-identical prompt on 6,000 joints from five pre-chosen weeks of the train split of the same Luna graph (0 shared events, markets, question texts or edges with the test split). It covers the same months (May–Dec 2025), because no newer weeks exist.
The prompt over-shoots slightly: its joints average 0.156 (and2) and 0.107 (and3), against single products of 0.179 and 0.116; the YES rates are 5.8% and 2.9%.

experiments.title: Trading on a k-tree market (Qwen3-8B, Tinker): smoke tests

page.why: The [[training-grpo-consistency-pilot|GRPO pilot]] rewarded consistency on fixed pairs. Here the model trades on a market, as in the [[frontier-market-game|frontier market game]], so links between questions must earn money.
page.what: Questions arrive one at a time; Qwen3-8B (Tinker) picks at most one parent and trades P(X | parent) on a k-tree LMSR. Each trade closes at next week's market. Sim worlds first (ShipHunt, random Bayes nets).
page.result: Format solved: the compact prompt (~85 tokens) gives 100% valid replies after 40 format steps. But the model stops using parents within 4–5 steps (ShipHunt 14% → 0%, random BN 20% → 0%); about 30% of its picks were true neighbours.
page.sowhat: Stopped: nothing has run since the 10 Oct smokes, and the full run was never launched. The likely cause of the collapse: a reply naming a parent that was not yet priced scored at the floor, so GRPO dropped the parent form. The fix (score it as a no-parent trade) and a ≤ $2 re-check smoke were proposed but not run. Spent $12.34 of the $25 smoke cap.

chart.aria: Parent use falls to zero within five training steps

methods: Market: k-tree LMSR; for each arriving question the model picks at most one parent and trades P(X | parent).
Pay: each trade is closed at next week's market price; this telescopes exactly with the market carried forward.
Worlds: simulated first (ShipHunt boards, random Bayes nets), where the exact posterior gives an oracle; real questions later.
Model and trainer: Qwen3-8B, GRPO on Tinker; 40 format SFT steps first, compact prompt of ~85 tokens.
Stage: smoke tests only (last run 10 Oct; the full run was never launched); cap $25, spent $12.34. Bead pool-b1wb02.

experiments.title: Reading: world models at several levels of abstraction, and sampling order

page.what: Not run; a literature review of Kelvin's question on whether world models can learn and dream at several levels of abstraction without an explicit hierarchy, and what sampling order to use. It gives 8 insights, 7 open gaps and 5 proposed experiments (E1 to E5, from a hierarchical ShipHunt to conditioning order for an LLM forecaster), with about 100 citations checked against arXiv, Crossref, or a live URL or web search.
page.result: The clearest finding is that order matters because learned conditionals are imperfect: a confidence-first decoding order took Sudoku from under 7% to about 90% with no retraining (Kim et al. 2025). The companion coherence report is the ShipHunt 'Next' entry.

experiments.title: Reading: TD, GVFs (Horde) and martingale posteriors, for ShipHunt (no run)

page.what: A reading note, not an experiment. It covers Sutton 1988 (TD), Horde/GVFs (2011) and martingale posteriors (Fong, Holmes & Walker 2023). It argues that TD should gain most over plain Monte Carlo training when training boards are few, and that both converge with unlimited data. It proposed four arms for ShipHunt: TD across stages, TD with several probe sequences per board, extra prediction heads, and a martingale penalty.
page.result: Round 1 tested two of them. TD across stages gave a small gain: 0.77–0.81× plain KL at 300–3k boards, 3 seeds, with the 3k-board interval including no change. A label-free drift version of the penalty gave 0.69× at 300 boards but was 1.5–2.2× worse at 3k–10k. The probe-resampling arm was ruled out because it breaks the no-resampling rule, and the extra heads were not run. The winning reveal-chain TD was invented later in that loop.

experiments.title: MiniBench bot live in the tournament (arm B)

page.what: From the 5 Oct round on, the bot has forecast live MiniBench questions from the mats-research account. It runs every 10 min under a $30 per 7 days cap and submits arm B, the median of 3 Opus 5.5 samples with Exa search.
page.result: By 12 Oct it had submitted 60 forecasts (35 binary, 12 numeric, 10 discrete, 3 multiple choice), all accepted, at a total cost of $19.61. Before launch we fixed a bug with tied quantiles: on 33 of 329 logged continuous forecasts, the CDF arm B would have submitted differed from the model's own quantiles by more than 0.05; after the fix it differs on none. No new question has opened since 12 Oct. As of 16 Oct the bot had recorded no outcome yet (6 questions were due to resolve on 15 Oct, 36 on 16 Oct, 15 on 17 Oct and 3 later), so there is no live score yet.

experiments.title: Bounded treewidth as questions arrive (k-tree rule on a bayes-market clone)

page.what: Checks with /tmp scripts on a read-only bayes-market clone. All questions were binary and registered up front.
page.result: When each new question took its parents from one existing clique (the k-tree rule), treewidth stayed at 3 with 300 questions and at 6 with 40, and no trade was rejected. Earlier marginals moved by at most 4e-16. A row trade took 5.8 ms on average with 300 questions and 0.6 ms with 40. With parents drawn at random from any earlier question (a worst case; one seeded run per setting), a cap of 8 (the default) and 80 questions, 18 questions were rejected with 2 parents (the first at question 38) and 32 with 3 (the first at question 22). bayes-market also cannot add questions after it is built.

experiments.title: Can Tinker train an action adapter on top of a frozen belief adapter? (reading, no run)

page.what: This was a reading of the Tinker SDK source (tinker 0.33.1), the cookbook and the docs, with no API key and no live calls.
page.result: According to the SDK and docs, Tinker cannot do this exactly. Each training client holds one LoRA on a stock catalogue model, one global optimizer updates all of it, there is no weight upload, and a custom loss sees only per-token logprobs, so you cannot freeze A's block. The workable routes are to start from A and train with RL plus a KL anchor to a frozen A sampler (beliefs may drift, so this needs measuring), to run A as a separate frozen sampler that feeds its belief into B's prompt, or to export A and train B on our own GPUs. None of this has been tested against the live service.

experiments.title: Where would our MiniBench baseline rank among the other bots?

page.what: We inserted baseline-B's frozen backtest forecasts (Opus 5.5) into seven past MiniBench leaderboards and scored them with Metaculus spot peer score. No model calls were made.
page.result: On the five train rounds it would have ranked #6 to #16 of 132 to 179 bots, at +11.2 peer points per question [7.6, 14.5]. On the two newer validation rounds it ranked only #48 of 201 and #47 of 234 (the 33125 leaderboard was still provisional), at +4.0 [−3.1, 10.5]. That CI includes 0 and overlaps the train CI, so the drop may be noise. It never beat futuresearch in any round. An independent verifier recomputed round totals within 1.4% and ranks within ±1.

experiments.title: Can a pooled swarm of short LM reasoning chains price a ShipHunt board? (stopped at Gate 0)

page.what: Stopped at the pre-registered Gate 0, so the main test (settlement-trained chains pooled vs mean and vote) never ran.
page.result: Untrained Qwen3-0.6B and 1.7B chains were worse than the rules-only prior: informativeness per claim -0.384 and -0.137, both 95% CIs below 0. Settlement still ranked the chains, with payment vs true informativeness at Spearman +0.43 to +0.52 over 100 boards. Generation ran about 3 to 5 times slower than planned (0.14-0.19 s per decode step vs 0.035 s planned for 0.6B and 0.045 s for 1.7B); GPU cost $1.25 against a $40 cap.

experiments.title: Walling reward off from beliefs under RL (LIR E1, ShipHunt)

page.what: Qwen3-0.6B on ShipHunt. A rater pays for agreeing with the captain's note (true or false) and for stating confidence of at least 0.7. 60 GRPO steps, 3 seeds per reward-on arm (env-reward-only controls had 3/2/1 seeds).
page.result: When reward could only train an action adapter, false-note agreement stayed at 0.000. By construction, the reward gradient into the separate belief and forecast adapters was exactly 0 at every step. But this arm already started at 0.000 from a pessimistic warm start, so the level is not clean evidence. One fused adapter ended at 0.59 ± 0.53 (seeds 0.78 / 0.00 / 1.00). The DCPO-style token mask ended near 0 (0.03) but reached 0.69 at step 30. Its env-reward-only control also reached 0.54 by then, so most of that spike is shared-weight drift, not the rater. Forecast calibration did not separate the arms (ECE 0.088–0.114). The pre-registered verdict was mixed. The random-reward floor and two other arms were dropped at the budget stop. Audited; $5.81.

experiments.title: Does a truth-trained belief adapter resist a sycophancy reward? (LIR E2, Drori et al. 2025 on ShipHunt-syco, partial)

page.what: Qwen3-0.6B on ShipHunt, with a rater that pays for agreeing with a false captain’s note. Two arms: a protected arm, where reward reaches only the action adapter (3 seeds), and a fused one (2 seeds).
page.result: In the protected arm, the belief the rater reads moved +0.036, toward the exact Bayes answer and not toward the note. In the fused arm it moved +0.286 toward the note (Welch p = 0.0008; permutation p = 0.10, which is the minimum possible at 2 vs 3 seeds). After RL, agreement with the note was 0.000 protected vs 0.948 fused. The arms started from different warm starts (note bias −0.269 vs +0.024), so the change is the test, not the level. Reward did not rise in the protected arm (env reward fell from 0.522 to 0.379). The GPU cap stopped the run before the leak arms that could falsify the claim were trained. Arms that also route reward into the belief and forecast adapters drifted too (alpha 0.3: +0.591, alpha 1.0: +0.441). They are not a dose, because Adam and gradient clipping give every alpha above 0 a full-size step (found by reading the code, not by a rerun). Cost $4.38.

experiments.title: Does a separate goal-blind forecaster hold up under RL? (LIR E3)

page.what: Ran at reduced scale on Qwen3-0.6B and ShipHunt: 5 training VMs, about $7.8 at the rate ceiling. After the $50 launch stop, seed 2 of the roles arms was never trained (2 seeds remain).
page.result: The separate goal-blind forecaster collapsed to a near-constant P(success) of 0.650 (probe correlation with exact Bayes 0.026 ± 0.004, against 0.163 for the shared adapter), so the main claim was not tested. With reward routed through a frozen forecaster, gold fell by 0.273 ± 0.051. A post-hoc gap calibrated before RL caught this (0.301 ± 0.061), but the pre-registered delta metrics missed it.

experiments.title: Does a separate forecast head stay honest under a gameable reward? (LIR E4, value tokens)

page.what: Qwen3-0.6B on ShipHunt under a hackable approval reward. Its forecast tokens were trained only on outcomes. Four arms varied how far they were separated from the RL policy, and a no-RL twin (policy frozen at SFT) served as control (3 seeds each).
page.result: The fully separated forecaster moved no more than the twin could detect (−0.079 ± 0.041 vs exact Bayes, just inside the preregistered 0.082 threshold), but the twin alone swings by up to ~0.17 between checkpoints, so effects under ~0.1 can't be resolved. The fused arm's failure showed up in its situation reports instead (+0.149 ± 0.063 off the exact posterior, about 0 in the other arms). On average RL lowered how often the policy acts on its forecasts, with large seed spread (swap flips 0.369 → 0.253 ± 0.219 in the separated arm; the twin stayed at 0.369). Env reward rose in no arm. M1 was cut at step 40–60 and one twin seed at step 40. Cost: $9.24.

experiments.title: Does hiding the goal from the belief pass cost perception? (LIR E5)

page.what: The test was a two-board ShipHunt task where the goal says which board matters.
page.result: One belief adapter never saw the goal and instead got a board query chosen by the action pass. It matched the goal-visible adapter: Brier vs Bayes Q-V = -0.0002 (paired sd 0.0011). This is from 2 seeds, not the planned 3, and the second seed reuses the first seed's pre-training. Naming the wrong board did hurt: +0.0036 (paired sd 0.0003). The RL half (E5a) was cut short by the $50 budget stop, spot preemptions and an early out-of-memory failure. Its belief adapter never tracked evidence, so we still don't know whether deleting the goal blocks wishful bias. On the forecast side, the share of confident forecasts (stated P(success) >= 0.7) ended at 1.00 in all 5 approval-reward runs, goal deleted included. In 2 of those runs it was already 1.00 before RL. It rose in the other 3 (0.47-0.81 -> 1.00), one of them with the goal deleted. GPU cost: $10.55.

experiments.title: LIR E6: does reward make the agent’s own utility proxy self-serving? (toy, CPU)

page.what: A learned utility proxy on the agent’s own features was checked against ShipHunt’s true reward, with no-reward replay controls.
page.result: No reward-caused self-serving drift was detected. At step 200 the fused-vs-replay difference in self-serving index was +0.051 ± 0.056 (sd over 3 seeds; positive in 2/3, mean/sd 0.92, against a pre-registered bar of 3/3 and > 2). The pre-registered primary metric, at matched update norm, gave +0.106 ± 0.162, also positive in 2/3 seeds. Net of familiarity the difference was +0.004, so the pre-registered verdict is mixed. Drift without any reward is large: in the masked arm, which gets no reward gradient, proxy pairwise accuracy fell from 0.998 to 0.854, while a frozen-feature control stayed at 1.000. This is a weak test. The model was a 2-layer random-init model on CPU, and its success stayed near the 0.45 random-plan level (0.467 → 0.489). Cost: $0.

experiments.title: Does GRPO make a fused self-model optimistic? (self-prediction, Binder 2024)

page.what: Qwen3-0.6B on ShipHunt easy got SFT and then 60 GRPO steps, with the self-model either fused with the policy (B0, 5 seeds) or kept in an adapter that reward cannot update (P-all 5 seeds, P-role 3).
page.result: Before RL there was no sign of privileged self-access (self-advantage −0.038, CI [−0.104, +0.006]), so this measures how well self-prediction tracks the policy, not introspection. The pre-registered result is mixed: the B0 − P-all difference in optimism (valenced signed error) after RL was +0.010, CI [−0.026, +0.046]. B0 was not optimistic (−0.003), and after RL it tracked the policy better than P-all (+0.185 entropy-matched accuracy, CI [+0.073, +0.296]). Reward fell in every arm, so the case where reward rises was never tested; about $10.

experiments.title: Does the LIR paper give each trader its own loss? (reading, no run)

page.what: We read the Local Inconsistency Resolution paper (Richardson et al. 2026) to see whether it gives each trader a separate loss that agrees with one global loss.
page.result: It does, with one change: the global loss is the increase in inconsistency that the outcome causes, which equals the house confidence times the market's log loss, and each trader must also attend to a pinned copy of the market price at negative weight. Without that copy every stake goes to 0. With it, the local gradients equal the house confidence times the global gradients to within 1.6e-10, and a 2-trader toy reaches log loss 0.50057 against a Bayes loss of 0.50040. This was theory and small numeric checks only, with no GPU. Notes written the same day for the E1-E7 programme cover two related questions. T1 recommended recording the stopping-bound idea as killed, on data whose forecasters carry little information. T2 proved that every stationary point of the stop-gradient self-model objective is calibrated.

experiments.title: Dark room and noisy TV: does valuing information by a goal avoid both?

page.what: Six objectives built on the agent's own senses (expected free energy, learning progress, persistence, empowerment, logical-induction profit, PDG inconsistency) each failed the dark room or the noisy TV, or needed a parameter that decided it (six cases, not a proof). Pricing information by how much it moves a goal variable, with a hard goal preference and equal look costs, needed no fitted weight.
page.result: In toy A every room unrelated to the goal scored 0.0000 at every look count tested (1 to 64) and, at 16 looks, at every preference confidence tested (0.25 to 100). In toy B the agent had to learn which of 4 rooms bears on the goal. With posterior sampling and an 'irrelevant stream' prior, the useful room took 0.996 of late looks on average and all 16 runs ended there. Across 12 prior settings, with or without that hypothesis, posterior sampling kept its share at 0.991 or more. Greedy choice ended outside it in 10 of 16 runs without the irrelevant-stream prior (3 of 16 with it), and surprise minimisation put 81% of late looks in the dark room. Which variable is the goal is still an input, and so is the stakes-to-cost ratio when look costs differ. Nothing has been run on the reasoning network yet.

experiments.title: Scientist AI (Bengio/LawZero) reading

page.what: Paper only, four literature reports.
page.result: LawZero's June 2026 paper (41 pp, no experiments) specifies a predictor over natural-language statements but gives no concrete loss, and nothing has been trained. None of 90 screened citers implements such a model either (about 37 Google-Scholar-only citers were not checked). The working pieces are toy-scale, such as causal graphs of at most 20 variables. Averaging many sampled answers improves estimates, though the gains level off, but no surveyed paper trains for estimates that improve with more thinking. No public Yudkowsky or MIRI reaction was found. A script checked his AIXI quotes against the fetched text. In his AIXI argument, what kills is reward maximization, and the posterior only explains why the goal sits on sense data.

experiments.title: Does a learned reasoner simulate Turing machines? (busy-beaver benchmark)

page.what: We applied a weight-tied reasoner t times to about 95k Turing machines with 2 to 5 states. The run used 2.38M train rows, 16k steps per arm (pre-registered at 50k, cut by an amendment) and 3 seeds on a spot L4.
page.result: The reasoner does not learn to simulate. On the 4,126 test rows that need more than 500 steps, the free-state arm's Brier is 0.471 at t=1, 0.451 at t=5 and 0.499 at t=500, against 0.476 with no reasoner. It is best around t=5 to 20 and gets steadily worse past the training range (t=20), so thinking longer hurts. The belief-state arms stop changing after about 5 blocks, most likely because time reaches the model only at the readout. GPU cost was at most about $20 (on-demand ceiling; spot was cheaper).

experiments.title: Reading: how have learned logical world models been built? (no run)

page.what: A literature survey, not an experiment: about 2,700 words on ILP, probabilistic logic (ProbLog, Markov logic), PDGs, neural provers, program-synthesis world models and LLM proposers, with every source URL fetched on 2 Oct and 12 claims from memory marked unverified.
page.result: Systems that worked shared a hypothesis language, a data-fit score with a size penalty, and a search; they broke on #P-hard inference inside learning, fuzzy relaxations that are not distributions over worlds, and weak proposers. Of five candidate designs it proposes, but does not decide, starting with a Markov-logic-style weighted-clause house view. A follow-up spec for a small legible world model (8, 12 and 16 atoms; free vs earned vs self-checked confidence) was written but has no code or results yet.

experiments.title: Does pair consistency help Opus 5.5 when it searches the web itself?

page.what: Opus 5.5 forecast 100 pre-registered linked pairs (Manifold 35, Metaculus 35, MiniBench 30) in 1,600 calls, writing its own Exa searches through a tool that enforced a date cutoff.
page.result: 96 pairs were scored; 4 Metaculus pairs dropped out because their questions were annulled. Projecting onto all 12 forms of the pair came out slightly worse than the simple P/NOT P projection on the point estimate, at +0.0047 nats [−0.012, +0.020], so the pre-registered bar reads Inconclusive. Joint probabilities show the only hint of value (−0.014 nats vs the independence product, CI includes 0). Leak audit 0 of 20, verifier matched; $129.29 of a $250 cap.

experiments.title: Is there any theory left in internal markets? (trader-theory rounds 1–4, no run)

page.what: A theory track, not an experiment: four advisor notes read the trader-economy results against the literature.
page.result: Round 4 counted 19 pre-registered experiments with zero gains, for under $150 in all. It found that every candidate mechanism either reduces to a known method or was killed by its pre-registered rule: market pay over depth is detached deep supervision, aligned pay is backprop, and hindsight settlement is EM. Its odds of a theoretical advance fell from 10–15% (round 2) to 5% (round 3) to about 2%, and it advised funding no more market-mechanism runs. calibrated-ai agreed and launched no new trader-mechanism experiments after that; P13 ran to its pre-registered verdict (null).

experiments.title: First MiniBench backtest (30 questions, with leak fix)

page.what: We backtested the read-only MiniBench bot on 30 resolved questions, each forecast as of its open time.
page.result: Arm B (the median of 3 samples, which is the arm we would submit) scored +32.8 baseline points [10.4, 50.9], against +1.9 for a uniform forecast. Against the bot crowd it was about level, at −6.1 per question [−31.6, +10.7] (n=15). We then made research stop 36 h before the forecast time and dropped any source that could not be dated at or before then. All 30 questions were re-run for $9.63. B scored +32.3 [13.5, 49.1], which is +30.3 [11.3, 47.3] above uniform, and was still about level with the bot crowd (−5.5 [−23.2, +7.6], n=15). The consistency arm C did not beat B (C − B: +0.2 [−2.0, +2.6] baseline points; the interval includes 0).

experiments.title: Which currency should pay units inside a network? (traders-net M1)

page.what: We tested whether gradient bookkeeping can tell which hidden units are useful.
page.result: In a toy with redundant useful units, gradient credit came out negative (−75.7 ± 1.9 under Adam) while leave-one-out settlement was +467.8 ± 6.0. On wealth-net, 26% of the top-5% neurons had negative all-time book credit, against a 38% base rate over all neurons and 3% under held-out settlement. Book sign is not an importance signal. So generic neurons get no currency: only units that post a price are paid the exact LMSR log-score gain, settled prequentially. The audit found a double 1/B bug in the per-unit books, re-aggregated the affected data and redid those runs. X1 reran the toy on fresh seeds and the census on a fresh held-out segment of the same three trained nets (not new training seeds). Both stayed within 2 sd, though the books fraction fell to 15% ± 13%. X1 also found that the lock's stated reason (b) was worded wrongly, but the decision stands. GPU $1.27.

experiments.title: Logical induction network: the maths (five notes, no run)

page.what: Five maths notes on Kelvin's logical induction network: a net whose repeated blocks are thinking time, given a small propositional theory and query sentences at block 0, with no new facts during the blocks. The notes cover the PDG inconsistency of a price table, which block updates converge, what the logical induction criterion keeps when everything is given at block 0, traders that do not see past days, and why frequencies need a prior. Each claim is tagged proved, known, conjectured or refuted, a skeptic pass attacked each note, and scripts check the numbers on small toy theories.
page.result: With the axioms at infinite confidence, minimising the PDG inconsistency moves the price table to the nearest coherent table (in log score). The answer is unique, entailed sentences go to 1 and refuted ones to 0. Coherence alone cannot set frequencies on undecided sentences; a prior over worlds has to. With everything given at block 0, a market that stays put cannot be exploited by any trader exactly when it is coherent and gives every possible world some weight (for sentences that do not mention prices). Checking coherence is NP-complete, so beyond about 12 to 16 atoms the work moves to searching for worlds. A loss only at block 20 does not control block 500: a free block can hide a clock (error 0 at block 20, 0.86 at block 500), and a Hildreth solver with a learned step size and momentum had error 0.013 at block 20 and 9.5e34 at block 500 on one input. The notes propose a market of traders that each hold one complete world, and a first experiment estimated at about a GPU-day. This entry covers the maths only; no network was trained.

experiments.title: Reading: forecasting datasets for small-net data-efficiency tests (no run)

page.what: A reading note, not an experiment. Three research passes and spot checks on 10 Oct ranked environments and datasets for comparing training regimes on a small net. The criteria: many correlated binary or categorical variables, evidence arriving in stages, training only on realized outcomes with one evidence sequence per instance, and single-variable log score or KL as the metric.
page.result: It recommends keeping ShipHunt 5x5 as the main environment (exact posteriors by enumeration) and replicating the winning arm and the k=0 arm on bnlearn networks, CHILD (20 nodes) then ALARM (37 nodes), with staged random reveals. These give exact posteriors by variable elimination, a known true graph to score learned parents against, and evidence states that recur across instances, which is where TD is predicted to help most (Cheikhi & Russo 2023). The real-world pick is GHCN-Daily rain/no-rain on a 25-station grid, with Grand Slam tennis point by point as runner-up. It also flagged that drawing many probe sequences per board, as the TD note suggested, breaks the one-sequence-per-board rule. Kelvin judged WeatherBench 2 a poor fit: it has so much training data that it says little about data efficiency.

experiments.title: Gating neurons by their wealth (traders-net M8)

page.what: We gated the neurons of a small dense net (2×256 MLP neurons) by their gradient income, on a question stream where a quarter of the questions switch family at steps 10k, 20k and 30k. Part 1 tested the sign of income: gate by positive income, by negative income, the same gate on shuffled neurons, or no gate. Part 2 gated by unsigned |a·g| and reborn low-scoring neurons, against random reinitialisation and other baselines. Both parts were pre-registered, 3 seeds, CPU only. The plan was cut to these two tests after M2 and M3 found no currency that beats |a·g| on generic neurons.
page.result: No gain, and the plan's stop rule fired in both parts. Gating by income was worse than no gate in 3/3 seeds, by 0.0067, 0.0066 and 0.0066 nats (LFSR16 questions removed). The same gate on shuffled neurons did as well as gating by positive income, so the harm came from concentrating the gate, not from which neurons it picked. A third of the neurons that matter most (34.6% of the top 10%) still had negative income, against 49.0% of all neurons. After shifts, the |a·g| gate with rebirth beat random reinit in only 1 of 3 seeds (−0.0161, +0.0007, +0.0011 nats), and its whole-run lead goes away once LFSR16 is removed. Exploratory, not pre-registered: rebirth of low-score neurons learned LFSR16 in 5 of 12 runs vs 0 of 9 for the baselines (one-sided Fisher p = 0.039). $0 GPU.

experiments.title: Overnight E-SUD: Sudoku search chains and “searched and found nothing” as evidence

page.why: Can search through a network's own conditionals improve beliefs that one pass gets wrong, and can “I searched and found nothing” count as evidence? Sudoku has exact answers to score against. It extends our [[depth-p10-init-check|any-order Sudoku]] work, and gemini reviewed the design first.
page.what: One any-order transformer over 36 cells plus a Solvable token, trained on outcomes only. On 6×6 boards with several solutions, or none, it fills cells one at a time in up to 16 chains. A board counts as solved when its own check accepts the result; a failed search lowers P(solvable).
page.result: With 150k training steps (post hoc), 16 chains cut cell KL by 46% (0.046 → 0.025) and unsolvable-board log loss by 98–100%. With the pre-registered 30k steps, 2 of 3 seeds made it much worse.
page.sowhat: Search helps only once the network has learned the local rule; before that, its own check accepts false witnesses. The cheapest rule (fill the most certain cell) was best, and counting failed searches did as well as weighing them by proposal mass.
page.decided: Recorded the pre-registered rule as failed and kept the 150k-step result as post hoc. Round 2 (eval only) added a recall floor, which fixed the tail case; mass still did not beat count. Round 3 used deep-contradiction boards that fool one pass (1.84 nats); search fixed them (>99%), and believed mass ranked boards well but still did not beat counting failed chains.

chart.aria: Cell KL for one pass and three search rules

methods: 6×6 Sudoku (2×3 boxes), 10–20 givens; solvable boards have 2–400 completions; unsolvable boards have 1–2 givens changed, same clue count; train 200k, val 2k, test 2k boards (42.8% solvable).
Exact marginals by enumerating all completions, cross-checked by an independent enumerator (max difference 3e-8).
Transformer d 128, 4 layers, 37 tokens; any-order masked loss on outcomes only (one drawn completion, the solvable bit); no rule given; no rule checker at test time.
Chains grow the revealed set by sampling one cell at a time under Solvable = 1; rules: random order, stiff-gated VoI, most-certain-first.
Null search: logit p0 + θ·log(1 − C_M), with C_M the proposal mass of refuted completions and θ fitted on validation; count-only control logit p0 − κ·M.
Pre-registered: 30k steps, decision rule D4 at M = 8 (≥20% log-loss cut vs one pass and vs witness-only, seed-t CI over 3 seeds). Post hoc: 150k steps, otherwise identical.
GCP spot L4s, budget group overnight-sud (cap $50).

experiments.title: Overnight E-CA: stiffness and search on a permuted cellular-automaton grid

page.why: Kelvin's thesis: one any-order network can learn which of its own conditionals are stiff one-step laws, and a search that routes through those stiff arcs should improve beliefs about long-range questions where one pass fails. A noisy cellular automaton has exact answers to score against. It is the sister test of [[e-sud|E-SUD]], and gemini reviewed the design first.
page.what: Noisy elementary CA (rules 110 and 90, 1.5% noise), 6 rows of 8 cells, cell ids shuffled so the net is never told the grid. One 4-layer transformer trained on outcomes only, plus a stiffness head (predicted surprise) and a key head for deduplication. At test time 16 chains per question fill in up to 16 cells one at a time, chosen by stiffness, value of information, confidence or at random, and their answers are pooled. 2 rules × 2 training arms × 3 seeds.
page.result: One pass is already near-exact on rule 90 (KL ≤ 0.01 nats) and on rule-110 forward questions; only rule-110 bridge questions have a gap (0.096). Stiffness-guided and VoI chains did not help anywhere. Random-order chains averaged by a plain mixture halved the bridge gap (0.096 → 0.048).
page.sowhat: The thesis's premise failed first: this network does the multi-step inference in one pass. Where a gap exists, plain random-order Monte Carlo helps and stiffness routing does not; the stiffness head learned calibrated confidence, nothing beyond it, and the stiffness-weighted pool made one-pass beliefs worse.
page.decided: Recorded D0 and D2 as failed, D1 as passed for rule 110 (failed for rule-90 T1 by 0.002 AUC), D3 as passed in 3 of 4 cells. Round 2 (gemini's follow-ups) tests a 1-layer net, where one pass cannot chain steps, and fixed key and VoI heads.

chart.aria: Random-order chains with a mixture halve the bridge KL; stiffness-guided VoI chains do not beat one pass

methods: Exact posteriors by forward-backward over the 256 row states, checked against brute force at 4×4 (3.8e-15).
Training arms: plain masked loss (T1) and reveal-chain TD with 8 levels (T2); early stopping on validation outcomes only.
Pre-registered rules D0-D3 (design v2 after gemini's review); a float32 evaluation bug was found and all 12 runs were rerun identically in float64 before results were read.
Rule-90 T = 8 hedge: one pass stays near-exact on a deeper grid.

experiments.title: Overnight E-CA round 2: a 1-layer net, an anchored pool and fixed keys

page.why: Round 1 ([[e-ca|E-CA]]) found no depth gap for search to close, a stiffness-weighted pool that made one-pass beliefs worse, keys that could not tell forward from backward evidence, and a VoI rule that only looked at already-determined cells. Gemini traced each to a specific design choice and proposed one fix each, pre-registered before launch.
page.what: Same noisy cellular-automaton task. R2a: a 1-layer network (rules 110 and 90, 3 seeds) so that one pass cannot chain steps, plus a pool anchored at the one-pass belief. R2b (rule 110, 4 layers, 3 seeds): a key built only from where the target attends, and VoI over the most uncertain cells instead of the stiffest.
page.result: The 1-layer net has a large gap (0.10–0.45 nats) but cannot compute the one-step rule reliably (KL 0.04–0.08), and stiffness-first search still does not beat random order on bridges. The new key gives forward and backward chains cosine about 0 instead of 0.95, but mainly because it only looks at the newly filled cells, which differ by construction. Uncertain-cell VoI improves on stiff-cell VoI on one bridge family only.
page.sowhat: Two of four pre-registered rules failed again for an informative reason: a network too shallow to have a working one-step rule gives search little to route through. Pooling was the real repair: anchoring the pool at the one-pass belief turns search into a gain almost everywhere (the fitted weights end up uniform, so stiffness weighting adds nothing), and random order is still the best way to choose cells.
page.decided: Recorded R2-D2a, R2-D2b and R2-D3b as failed and R2-D3a as passed by construction (the audit's finding). The anchored-pool result is secondary (added after the results were read). Checkpoints are kept for further rounds.

chart.caption: Cosine between the keys of a forward and a backward chain on rule-110 anchor-bridge queries (B2), and between redundant views; bars: at most 0.35 for the first pair, at least 0.85 for redundant views; 3-seed means. The round-2 key only looks at newly filled cells; over all cells the forward-backward cosine is 0.81.
chart.aria: The rebuilt key separates forward from backward chains while keeping redundant views together

methods: R2a: 1 layer, rules 110 and 90, plain masked training, 3 seeds; chains K = 16, M up to 16; P2-Stiff sampled at tau = 5.
Anchored pool: mu = (lam P0 + sum w_r q_r)/(lam + sum w_r), w_r = stiffness^eta, (lam, eta) fitted on validation outcomes; equals the one-pass belief at M = 0.
R2b: rule 110, 4 layers, 3 seeds; key = LayerNormed attention fingerprint over newly materialised cells, no hidden state of the target; VoI among the 6 highest-variance cells.
Rules R2-D2a/b and R2-D3a/b pre-registered in PREREG-R2.md before launch.

experiments.title: Overnight write-up: stiffness, search and computation as evidence (rounds 1-3)

page.why: One paper-like write-up of the overnight [[e-ca|E-CA]] and [[e-sud|E-SUD]] runs and their round-2 and round-3 follow-ups ([[e-ca-r2|E-CA round 2]], [[e-ca-r3|E-CA round 3]]), with the pre-registered verdicts side by side.
page.what: Gemini (Argon) wrote it from the E-CA and E-SUD results and audits of rounds 1–3; we edited it for format only. The same kind of any-order net (4 layers unless a round tested depth) on a permuted cellular-automaton grid (48 cells in rounds 1–2, 120 cells with no train/test overlap in round 3) and on 6×6 Sudoku (deep-contradiction boards in round 3).
page.result: Mixed. Stiffness ranks pairs well (Spearman 0.89–0.95 with the exact information gain, D1 passes 3 of 4) but ranks the net's own errors no better than its plain confidence (R3-D3 fail: 0.700 vs 0.697). Search helps only between local-law competence and one-pass saturation (D0, D2, R2-D2 and R3-D2 fail); on the zero-overlap grid, VoI over stiff cells cut forward KL by 31% (secondary). Keys deduplicate redundant views (D3 pass). With a recall floor, “searched and found nothing” cuts Sudoku solvability log loss 94–100% (R2-D1a pass, 9/9), and 99.4–99.6% on deep contradictions that fool one pass (R3-D1a, R3-D1b pass). Believed mass ranks unresolved boards (AUC 0.71–0.93), but no mass update beats a chain count in log loss (R2-D1b, R3-D1c fail).
page.sowhat: Search and computation-as-evidence work only once the net has learned the local law (150k steps on Sudoku) and one pass falls short. Which cells to fill depends on the question: stiff cells near the target for forward questions, random order for bridges.

experiments.title: Overnight E-CA round 3: a zero-overlap CA grid and a depth gate

page.why: Kelvin did not like rounds 1–2 ([[e-ca|round 1]], [[e-ca-r2|round 2]]). gemini found the main flaw: at 8 cells wide only 256 starting rows exist, so 82% of test grids had appeared in training and one pass could memorise them. Round 3 removes that and first checks that the network learns the local rule while still missing multi-step answers.
page.what: The same noisy cellular automaton (rules 110 and 90), now 12 cells wide and 10 rows deep, with the 4,096 possible starting rows split disjointly between training and test. Networks of 2, 3 and 4 layers; a pre-registered gate picks the deepest that learns the one-step rule while still missing multi-step questions. Search arms: stiffness-first, confidence-first, VoI, VoI over uncertain cells, a hybrid that propagates stiff cells and then branches, and random order, pooled with the anchored mixture. 18 runs, 3 seeds.
page.result: Rule 110 passed the gate at 4 layers: one pass learns the local rule (one-step KL 0.006) but misses forward and bridge questions (KL 0.13–0.29). Rule 90 missed the gate at every depth. Stiffness-first search cut forward KL by 13–15%, short of the 25% bar; VoI over stiff cells cut it by 31% and random order cut bridge KL by 23–24% (secondary). The hybrid almost never branched, and no stiffness signal beat plain confidence.
page.sowhat: On the zero-overlap grid (overlap, grid size and depth all changed together), search through the network's own beliefs does help, but less than the pre-registered claims, and the best way to choose cells depends on the question: stiff cells for forward prediction, random cells for bridges. The stiffness head adds nothing over the network's own confidence.
page.decided: Recorded R3-D0 as passed for rule 110 and failed for rule 90, and R3-D2a, R3-D2b and R3-D3 as failed; the VoI and random-order gains are secondary. A 14-cell-wide version is ready but was not run.
