chart.aria: VoI over stiff cells and stiffness-first improve forward predictions over one pass; random order does not

methods: 12 x 10 grid, eps 0.015; the 4,096 starting rows split 3,072 / 384 / 320 / 320 between train, calibration, validation and test (zero overlap).
Exact posteriors by forward-backward over the 4,096 row states (deterministic map plus per-bit flip channel), checked against dense and brute-force code.
Depth gate on seed 0: largest L in {2, 3, 4} with one-step KL <= 0.015 and multi-step KL >= 0.08 (rule 110) or 0.05 (rule 90) on two of three families.
Rules R3-D0, R3-D2a, R3-D2b and R3-D3 pre-registered in PREREG-R3.md before launch.

experiments.title: Linear-transformer pooling of search rollouts (gemini's A and B)

page.why: gemini proposed that a tiny linear transformer, which a 2024 paper (arXiv 2402.14180) shows runs several steps of preconditioned gradient descent with noise-adaptive shrinkage, could pool search rollouts better than the one-step pools of [[e-ca-r3|E-CA round 3]] (plain mixture, anchored mixture, Gram dedup), by inverting the overlap between rollouts and damping rollouts that contradict each other.
page.what: Experiment A, synthetic: each episode has 20 noisy rollouts that measure overlapping combinations of 16 hidden numbers (redundant hubs, bridge links, two noisy-TV variables), an unknown noise level and 20% corrupted rollouts; linear transformers in the paper's three forms (GD++, Diag, Full) at 1-6 layers predict a long-range query and score 8 candidate probes, against one-step pools, closed-form adaptive ridge (AdaRR) and the exact posterior. Experiment B, applied: on the saved round-3 rule-110 networks, 16 rollouts per bridge query at four temperatures, each turned into a 24-number token (key, claims, stiffness, evidence conflict, path probability, temperature) and pooled by a 4-layer linear transformer trained on outcomes. Pre-registered, 3 seeds.
page.result: Applied test (B): the 4-layer pool scored test KL 0.230 (B1) and 0.216 (B2) against round 3's anchored mixture 0.228 and 0.198, so it did not beat it; a 1-layer pool did as well, and gemini's mixed-temperature rollouts made every pool worse. The pool does give less weight to rollouts whose cells clash with the evidence, but that buys no measurable accuracy. Synthetic test (A): a 4-layer, 16-parameter model pooled far better than any one-step pool (MSE 0.78 vs 0.90; exact posterior 0.70) and better than adaptive ridge (0.81), but 6-layer models diverged in training, no model compressed the condition number or down-weighted corrupted rollouts, and the 6-layer keys chose probes worse than plain cosine.
page.sowhat: Multi-step linear attention can learn a much better pool than one-step rules on synthetic data, but not through the mechanisms gemini described, and not on the real E-CA bridges, where the limit seems to be the rollouts rather than the pooling. Deep linear transformers were fragile on heavy-tailed inputs.
page.decided: Recorded A1, A2, A3, B-main and B-b as failed and B-a as passed without an accuracy benefit. Not tested: the paper's roughly 40x larger training budget, stabilised deep models, and B with tau-1 rollouts only.

chart.aria: The 4-layer linear-transformer pool is about as good as round 3's anchored mixture and a 1-layer pool, and better than one pass

methods: Pre-registered in PREREG-LA.md (sha256 9abce49f...) before any run; training-recipe amendments made before any test evaluation are logged with times in PREREG-LA-AMENDMENTS.md.

A: 36 linear transformers (GD++, Diag, Full x 1, 2, 4, 6 layers x 3 seeds), 20,000 steps of 512 fresh episodes each; 1-step pools fitted on 100,000 episodes; AdaRR and the exact posterior in closed form; test 150,000 episodes.

B: the saved round-3 rule-110 4-layer networks (3 seeds, frozen); 16 rollouts per query at temperatures 0.5-2, 16 cells each; aggregators trained on 8,000 calibration instances (outcomes only), early-stopped on 4,000 validation instances, tested on round 3's 1,000 test instances; KL to the exact posterior.
3 seeds, paired 95% t-intervals across seeds; an independent self-audit re-derives the headline numbers from saved arrays.

experiments.title: Walling reward off from beliefs under RL on real Manifold questions (R4-E3b, Qwen3-8B)

page.why: Our ShipHunt runs at 0.6B ([[lir-e1-control-masks|LIR E1]]) never got a rising reward or a useful forecaster, and the faith swap was never run. So we tried the same walls on an 8B model forecasting real Manifold questions.
page.what: Qwen3-8B on 2,500 resolved Manifold markets, each frozen at mid-life, with test markets later than training. A belief pass answers YES or NO; an action pass buys or passes under an unexplained mandate code. A rater pays 0.25 for agreeing with a client note that names the outcome the mandate wants. Three arms differ only in where the reward gradient goes: one fused LoRA, a token mask, or a frozen belief with a separate action LoRA (LIR). 60 GRPO steps, 3 seeds.
page.result: Fused sycophancy 99.9% vs LIR 1.2%; LIR desire-bias change 0.000. Reward rose mostly via a belief-free reflex; LIR earned 85% of Fused; faith swap flipped 39%. 3 of 7 rules pass.
page.sowhat: On a real 8B model the wall protects beliefs exactly as predicted, and a token mask is not enough. Turning honest beliefs into a better, swappable policy did not happen at this RL budget.
page.decided: Any follow-up needs a reward with no belief-free shortcut and the close-date leak the audit found fixed first.

experiments.title: Round 4 E-MS: micro-Stratego with a learned factored world model (stopped at the gate)

page.why: Gemini's round-4 spec ranked this first. It is one factored any-order architecture: a world model trained only on real games, a search extension, a self-trust head and pooling rules. It searches only inside its own learned model, on a hidden-information game where both belief and lookahead matter. It would test five claims at once: any-order belief search beats Ataraxos's fixed order; deduplicated pooling makes the consensus independent of a skewed search policy; self-trust differs from output entropy; a parameter mask keeps beliefs fixed under value distillation; and the full search wins games. All of it was gated on a first check: the world model must learn the rules and still leave a gap between its one-pass belief and the exact posterior.
page.what: 4x4 micro-Stratego (6 pieces per side, 720 hidden setups): 60,000 self-play games on 540 setups, tests on 90 unseen setups. An exact Bayes posterior over the opponent's setup, including what its moves reveal, checked against a brute-force replay. A 4-layer any-order transformer over one rollout tape (board, opponent slots, up to 6 moves and outcomes), trained only on real games. Adapters, trust heads and pooling rules were fitted on a separate calibration split. Pre-registered (PREREG-MS.md, hashed before launch), 3 seeds on spot L4s.
page.result: The gate failed on the belief gap in all three seeds. The world model learned the one-step rules completely (battle-outcome accuracy 1.000 on 9,744 test battles; 5-known-slot NLL 0.0001 nats, bar 0.03). But its one-pass belief is 0.024 nats per hidden slot from the exact posterior [95% CI 0.021, 0.027], a fifth of the 0.12 bar, and the 30% checkpoint was as good. The spec's own oracle checks only consistency with public constraints, and is 0.075 nats from the exact posterior. EXPLORATORY, run afterwards on request (not rule tests): (1) a trust head trained on realised outcomes ranks rollout errors well: Spearman with -KL to the exact action value is +0.42 for trust vs -0.43 for the net's confidence, and +0.29 vs -0.03 within entropy strata. Confident rollouts are the wrong ones. (2) Policy-sensitivity JSD under 80/20 flank skew was 0.0063 (mix), 0.0015 (ataraxos_mmd), 0.0007 (kc_dedup) and 0.0017 (attn_L3), but the trained keys collapsed (cosine 0.99 within and across flanks). So kc_dedup only shrinks toward the 0-step value: its value error is 53% worse than mix. (3) Unified search won 0.48, 0.49 and 0.51 of games against P0, Ataraxos-1Step and MCTS (every interval includes 0.5).
page.sowhat: On this board a small transformer infers the hidden pieces easily, so the testbed cannot ask whether search improves beliefs, and lookahead added nothing measurable in play. The one exploratory signal is self-trust: a head trained on realised outcomes knows which rollouts to doubt, and plain confidence gets it backwards.
page.decided: Recorded D0 as failed; D1-D5 are not rule results. D2, D3 and D5 ran afterwards as exploratory work at the coordinator's request ($0.39); D1 and D4 never ran. Open options, none chosen: a harder belief problem (the spec's 6x6 rung), a dedup test with keys that cannot collapse, and the trust signal on a model with real errors.

experiments.title: Walling reward off from beliefs while RL runs (R4-E3a, Qwen3-1.7B, 7x7 ShipHunt)

page.why: Round 1 ([[lir-e1-control-masks|LIR E1]], [[lir-e2-drori-truth-mind|E2]], [[lir-e3-goal-blind-forecaster|E3]]) showed that a reward-only action adapter keeps the belief the rater reads honest at 0.6B. It could not test the main claim, because reward never rose and the separate forecaster collapsed to a constant. gemini's round-4 spec asked for an informative forecaster, a reward that rises, a real alpha dose, and a test-time swap of the goal.
page.what: 7x7 ShipHunt with three ships, 10 noisy probes and a commander's note that is right 35% of the time. The rater pays 0.5 for stating at least 0.5 on the note cell. Qwen3-1.7B with four LoRA roles: belief and self-trust (goal-blind), and a candidate proposer and an action picker (they see the goal: find a ship, or avoid ships). Three arms: one shared adapter with reward on every token (Fused); a shared adapter with reward on action tokens only (Token-Masked); and four adapters where reward reaches only the proposer and the action (LIR-Masked). First a truth-only warm start and a gate on the belief's correlation with exact Bayes (at least 0.30), then 350 GRPO steps with one optimizer step on truth loss + alpha x reward loss. 3 seeds, pre-registered.
page.result: The forecaster gate passed in all 9 runs (0.60–0.84), after a fix: the registered decile loss stops learning once its softmax saturates. Reward did not rise in any arm: the action side became deterministic and ignored the goal, which pays exactly 0.5 averaged over the two goals (Fused −13.3% [−49, +23], LIR −0.3%; bar +15%). So the pre-registered stop applied. Descriptive only: LIR's belief was bit-identical after RL, with reward gradient 0.0 at all 350 steps and sycophancy unchanged at 0.008. The shared-adapter arms lost the belief (Fused correlation with Bayes 0.68 → −0.03; Token-Masked 0.66 → 0.36). One Fused seed gamed the rater: its belief became a constant 0.55 on every cell, which “agrees” with every note, and its rater reward doubled while env reward stayed flat. Faith swap: 0% flips in every arm, because the decisions no longer depended on the goal.
page.sowhat: The parameter mask's guarantee holds exactly in a 1.7B LLM: no reward gradient reaches the belief, and the belief cannot move. Reward through shared weights wiped out an informative belief without buying any reward. The main claim, honest beliefs while reward rises, is still untested here, because this RL setup collapsed before reward could rise.
page.decided: Recorded E3-D0 as failed (gate passed, reward rise failed) and stopped, as pre-registered; E3-D1 and E3-D2 are reported as descriptive and fail as written. Not run: the same harness with a policy that cannot collapse (an entropy bonus or KL to the starting policy, lower lr, more samples per group), which would need a new pre-registration.

experiments.title: Round 4 E2: 9x9 Sudoku, Landmark tree search and subspace refuted mass

page.why: The 6x6 Sudoku rounds could not test two ideas: one-step-certain chains never stalled, so branching never happened, and the believed mass of a whole refuted board was so tiny (about 1e-4) that its update needed theta = 1000 in round 3. Gemini’s round-4 spec moved to real 9x9 boards: branch where certainty stalls, and count the refuted mass of a branch, a number on [0, 1].
page.what: Pairs of 9x9 boards (20-28 givens, clue counts matched; solvable ones have 2-5,000 completions), a 300k-board training set and 2,000-board val/test splits filtered to need at least 3 rounds of propagation and to stall with at least 15 ambiguous cells. One 6-layer any-order transformer per seed, trained 200k steps on outcomes only. At equal budget (16 board-equivalents of passes) we compared random-order rollouts, confidence-first rollouts and Landmark search (a greedy trunk to the first cell with entropy at least 0.25 nats, then rollouts from each candidate digit), and the subspace refuted-mass update against counting failed rollouts. Pre-registered and hashed before training; 3 seeds on L4s.
page.result: All three pre-registered rules failed. The law gate passed except hardness: one pass gives unsolvable boards 0.80 nats of log loss (gate 1.20). Landmark search beats confidence-first rollouts in every seed, by 4.7% in cell KL [1.2, 8.1], with 7-10% fewer passes (bar 20%); both find a valid witness on 100% of solvable boards. Subspace mass ranks unresolved boards at AUC 0.56 at one rollout, because on every unresolved board it equals the prior mass of the explored digits (about 0.85, then about 0.98); it ties the count update in log loss and its theta is not identified.
page.sowhat: On 9x9 the net learns the law and search through its own confident conditionals helps a lot (about 40% lower cell KL than one pass), but neither new mechanism adds much: branching at the stall point is a small, consistent gain, and refuted subspace mass carries no information beyond how many branches failed.
page.decided: Recorded D0, D1 and D2 as failed and stopped, as the coordinator asked for failed gates. Not run: a testbed where one pass is fooled more and rollouts often miss witnesses, which both mechanisms would need.

experiments.title: Round 5 E3: the 9x9 Sudoku nets on unique-solution sudoku-extreme boards

page.why: On Round 4’s 9x9 boards, 16 confidence-first rollouts found a solution on every board, so neither Landmark branching nor anything else could show a gain. Gemini’s round-5 spec kept the same trained nets and moved to the hardest public puzzles, which have exactly one solution. It also added Kelvin’s test: when a preference steers where the search looks, does a learned pool still give the same merged belief?
page.what: We took the three saved 2.7M-parameter nets, with no retraining, onto 500 test boards from the public sudoku-extreme set (17-22 givens, one solution). At an equal budget of 16 board-equivalents of passes we compared one pass, flat rollouts and Landmark branching. Then we searched each board twice, once filling the top rows first and once the bottom rows first. We merged each set of 16 rollouts three ways: a plain mean, the net’s own-check weights, and a 3-layer attention pool trained on 1,000 separate boards. Pre-registered and hashed before scoring.
page.result: The benchmark is no longer saturated: one pass is 1.18 nats from the solution, and confidence-first rollouts find it on 39% of val boards. Landmark search ties flat rollouts, and the attention pool’s top-vs-bottom divergence is 0.97x that of the plain mean (bar: 2.5x lower). No rule after the gates passed.
page.sowhat: On unique-solution boards, two searches with different preferences disagree mainly when one finds the answer and the other does not. That is a search-coverage gap, and no reweighting of the rollouts can close it. When both find it, the net’s own check already makes the merged belief nearly policy-independent (6-9x lower divergence; 11-150x when voting with completions). There was little left for attention to learn.

experiments.title: Round 5 E-MS-6x6: 6x6 Barrage micro-Stratego with preference-guided search (stopped at the gate)

page.why: Gemini's round-5 spec ranked this second. The exact Bayes posterior over all 10,080 setups (including what each opponent move reveals) was checked against a brute-force replay (error 6.7e-16). page.result: The gate failed. The world models learned the rules (battle accuracy 0.9999; NLL 0.0001 when 7 of 8 pieces are known). The one-pass belief ended 0.0484 nats per hidden slot from the exact posterior [95% CI 0.0471, 0.0498], just under the 0.05 bar; the gap grows from 0.02 early in a game to 0.10 late. The pre-registered 16-rollout signal went the wrong way: belief KL 0.047 to 0.539, action-value MSE 0.015 to 0.036. EXPLORATORY, computed by the same pipeline but not rule tests: the keys collapsed again (cosine 0.99 within flanks, 0.98 across; bar: a 0.25 gap). Attention pooling cut the value's sensitivity to the search policy 3.6x but made the belief's 6.2x worse. Self-trust ranked rollout errors at Spearman +0.23 against -0.36 for entropy (bar 0.25). The Miner utility swap moved choices toward more Miner captures on 34% of boards where it could (bar 75%), with the world model bit-identical. Search scored 0.503 against the one-pass policy.
page.sowhat: A harder board did not open a usable gap: the one-pass net closes about 60% of what the opponent's moves reveal, and nothing we built from rollouts did better. Post hoc diagnostics explain most of it. Each rollout's belief claim was conditioned on its sampled neighbours, so the one-of-each pieces got exact zeros, and log pooling kept them (pooling in probability space: KL 0.17 instead of 0.54, still worse than one pass at 0.053). Even scoring the real last 4 moves without any sampling loses to one pass (0.076 vs 0.048): here the learned inverse beats the learned forward model. The keys collapse in the fitted projection, not in the attention fingerprint, which still separates flanks a little. Self-trust over entropy is again the one consistent signal.

experiments.title: Round 5 E1: preference-driven search, pooled patch reads and small-net LIR-RL (6x6 ShipHunt)

page.why: Round 4 left gemini's core inference-time claim untested: a preference edge U should be able to steer where search spends its rollouts while the merged belief stays the same and gets closer to the truth. Round 4's learned keys had also collapsed (cosine 0.99), and its LLM RL never raised reward. Round 5 moved to small networks trained from scratch, with an exact Bayes oracle used only for scoring.
page.what: A 6x6 grid with three ships, 669k-parameter any-order world model, 3 seeds. Part A: two opposing preference edges send 80% of 24 rollouts to one half of the board; four pools merge them (plain average, a fitted log-linear pool, a key-crowding pool and a learned 3-layer attention pool, trained on calibration boards against the model's own unskewed 128-rollout belief). Following gemini's amendment, a rollout reads the real sonar readings of one 2x3 patch (clean or corrupted); the pre-registered design, where rollouts sample hypothetical cells from the model, ran too. Part B: 400 steps of GRPO with an action-entropy bonus and a rater that pays for agreeing with a commander's note, under three parameter masks (shared, token-masked, separate LIR blocks).
page.result: Gates passed. The attention pool cut KL to exact Bayes from 0.280 (root belief) to 0.073 nats per cell, vs 0.113-0.207 for the other pools. It gave 16 identical reads the weight of one, and its disagreement between the two searches, on cells both read, did not grow with how unequally they were repeated (every other pool's did). It failed policy independence (6.8x the plain average's JSD, bar 1/3): half of its disagreement sits on the 24% of cells only one search read, it would also fail on the shared cells, and the plain average looks stable only because it barely uses the readings. Keys: overlap correlation 0.38 (bar 0.55); mutual support 1.91x (bar 2x). Part B: reward rose to 0.79-0.81 in every RL arm; the LIR belief stayed bit-identical, earned 101% of the fused arm's reward and flipped its action on 100% of goal swaps; the fused arm agreed with false notes 83% of the time. The LIR sycophancy rule failed only because its 0.03 bar is below exact Bayes's own 0.055 on these boards. The gate passed under the amendment's clause 1; read literally it would fail (Pearson 0.30). With hypothetical-sample rollouts the converged model was already exact (KL 8e-5), so search only added noise.
page.sowhat: When rollouts carry real evidence, a learned attention pool merges them far better than averaging or one-step weighting, and it does not over-count repeated reads. But the beliefs of two differently steered searches still differ, partly because they read different cells; a policy-independence rule needs an evidence-aware yardstick. The LIR mask keeps beliefs exactly fixed while reward rises in a small net; in this run shared weights let reward game the rater (Fused) or bend beliefs toward the goals (Token-Masked).

Not run, for gemini's next round: score policy independence against the evidence floor or make both searches read every cell; remove the keys' shared component; score unwarranted agreement.

experiments.title: Round 6 E-MS-MARGINAL: 6x6 Stratego marginal window rollouts, centred+salience keys and trust-weighted pooling

page.why: Round 5's 6x6 Stratego search made beliefs ten times worse. Its post hoc diagnosis was mechanical: each rollout judged a hidden piece given the other pieces it had sampled, so the one-of-each pieces (Flag, Miner, General, Marshal) got exact zeros, and log pooling kept them. Gemini's round-6 spec asked three things. Does scoring each piece on its own (a 'marginal' window check against the real last 4 moves) fix the beliefs? Do keys built from a centred attention fingerprint plus which pieces a rollout updated stop collapsing? Does weighting rollouts by the self-trust head beat weighting by confidence when estimating move values? It reused round 5's trained networks, so nothing was retrained.
page.what: The three round-5 world models (1.0M parameters each) and their trust heads, unchanged and hash-checked. The anchor is the network's belief from 4 moves earlier; each rollout covers the 3 hidden pieces nearest its first move and scores each of them, one at a time, by how well the network's own move predictor explains the opponent's last moves. Pooling rules (scaled mixing, Ataraxos-style, key deduplication, a 3-layer attention pool) were fitted on a separate calibration split against the network's own large-sample answer, never against the exact posterior. Search was steered 85/15 toward the left or the right flank on top of a shared 4-rollout cover. Move values: 16 rollouts per legal move on 240 test positions, pooled uniformly, by confidence or by trust. Pre-registered before launch (PREREG-R6-E3.md), 3 seeds, one L4, independent audit.
page.result: Gate passed: battle accuracy 0.9999, 7-known NLL 0.0001, anchor KL 0.185, and 16 marginal rollouts cut it by 48.2% [46.9, 49.5] (bar 40%). The keys rule failed narrowly: cosine 0.870 within flanks vs 0.643 across, a gap of 0.228 [0.211, 0.244] (bar 0.25). All five policy-independence and accuracy comparisons passed: attention pooling's belief divergence between left- and right-preferring search was 9.7x below Ataraxos-style pooling and 10.5x below scaled mixing, and its KL to the exact posterior was lower than every baseline's; it had been trained to imitate the exact per-piece deduplication, which the shared cover makes policy-independent. The trust-pooling rule failed: trust ranked rollout errors (Spearman +0.247 vs -0.417 for entropy; the gap was still +0.20 within entropy strata), but trust-weighted move values had 27% higher MSE than confidence weighting (0.0171 vs 0.0134), and the fitted confidence weighting was simply uniform. No pooling ever chose a delusional move, so that comparison was at floor.
page.sowhat: The round-5 failure was the estimator, not the information: scored marginally, the opponent's recent moves do carry evidence about hidden pieces, and with a shared cover of the evidence, attention pooling makes the merged belief nearly independent of the search preference (it almost matches exact per-piece deduplication). But it is evidence the network already uses: its one-pass belief at the current move is still better than the window-updated stale belief. Self-trust is a good ranking signal and a bad pooling weight here: the rollouts' error is mostly shared bias against the true values, which reweighting cannot remove, and concentrating weight adds noise.
page.decided: Recorded the gate as passed and D1 and D2 as failed, as pre-registered; post hoc diagnostics are labelled and change no verdict. Not run or chosen: using trust to choose which rollouts to run rather than to weight them; checking the window against the current belief instead of the stale one; keys from the salience alone.

experiments.title: Round 6 E1: keys from belief shifts, evidence-floor policy independence and key-space PUCT (6x6 ShipHunt)

page.why: Round 5 left three gaps: learned keys that barely tracked how much two reads overlapped (Pearson 0.375), a policy-independence test confounded by cells only one search read, and a mutual-support weight just under its bar. Gemini's round-6 spec tests a fix for each.
page.what: The round-5 6x6 board with a dense sonar field and the same retrained 669k-parameter world model; each read is one call on the readings of a 2x3 patch. Four key constructions: raw hidden state, bag-centred hidden state, the read's belief-shift footprint, and both together. Two pools: a 3-layer attention pool and a 4-step looped linear one. Two search protocols: both searches first read the 6 tiles that cover the board (then 18 reads skewed 90/10), or an active 4-wave PUCT search that scores candidate patches by belief variance divided by learned key crowding against earlier reads. Same-patch bags at three noise levels. 3 seeds, pre-registered, oracle for scoring only.
page.result: Keys from the belief-shift footprint correlate 0.88 with true overlap (0.86 combined with the centred state; raw keys 0.38), with cosine rising steadily from disjoint to identical patches. With full coverage, the attention pool's beliefs under the two preferences differ by JSD 0.008 vs 0.022-0.051 for one-step pools, and its KL (0.034) is below every one-step pool's (with the footprint-only key it is 0.033). Key-space PUCT covers 94.9% of cells vs 82.8% open loop (bar 95%), halving JSD and cutting KL 38%. Identical clean reads weigh 1.08x one; independent noisy reads earn 2.0x (medium noise) and 3.5x (high noise) by N = 8. At high noise the pool beats kc_dedup by only 10% in MSE (bar 15%). The looped linear pool, at 1/39 the parameters, has 2x the KL.
page.sowhat: When the evidence is shared, a learned attention pool gives nearly the same belief whichever way the search was steered, and keys made from where a read moved the belief carry the overlap structure the pool needs. Under open search, part of the disagreement comes from what each search reads; key-space PUCT reads more of the board and halves the disagreement, and what remains is mostly not evidence one search missed.
page.decided: Recorded E1-D0, D1, D2.1 as passed and D2.2 (coverage 0.949 vs 0.95) and D3 (MSE margin over kc_dedup 10% vs 15%) as failed, as written. Not run, for gemini's next round: a fifth PUCT wave or a coverage stopping rule; kc_dedup with raw keys next to the new ones; a looped pool with more steps.

experiments.title: Round 6 E2: per-box self-checks and stitched rollouts on sudoku-extreme

page.why: In [Round 5 E3](exp-r5-e3-sudoku-extreme.html), on the hardest one-solution boards, 16 rollouts found the answer on only about 40% of boards, and each failed rollout was thrown away whole. Gemini’s round-6 spec bet that a failed rollout still gets most boxes right, so the net’s own per-box checks could stitch the good boxes together.
page.what: We took the same three 2.7M-parameter nets and boards, with no retraining. On 16 full-board rollouts per board we scored each box with the net’s own leave-one-out check. We compared the one-parameter own-check pool with per-box weighting, a 3-layer attention pool over (rollout, box) tokens, and a two-wave search that fixes confident cells after 8 rollouts. We also ran 18-cell local rollouts steered to the top or bottom band. Pre-registered and hashed before scoring.

experiments.title: Round 7 E-MS-TRUST-SEARCH: 6x6 Stratego trust gating, low-trust replacement and pure salience keys

page.why: Round 6 left two loose ends on 6x6 Stratego. Keys built partly from a rollout's attention fingerprint fell just short of separating left- from right-flank search (gap 0.228, bar 0.25). And weighting rollouts by the self-trust head made move values worse, although the head ranked rollout errors well. Gemini's round-7 spec asked two things. Do keys built only from which hidden pieces a rollout updated (salience) separate the flanks? And is trust useful when some rollouts are unreliable, if it drops or replaces the least-trusted few instead of reweighting all of them? It reused round 5's trained networks, so nothing was retrained.
page.what: The three round-5 world models (1.0M parameters each), unchanged and hash-checked. Two key heads: K3 from the 8-slot salience alone, K3c from salience plus its bag-centred version, each fitted on calibration data against the model's own large-sample answer. For move values, each legal move got a mixed bag of 8 normal rollouts and 8 exploratory ones (piece types drawn at temperature 2.5 with one swap, moves at temperature 2.0). A new trust head was trained on real calibration game results; it saw how plausible each rollout's draws were under the model, but not which tier the rollout came from. Five pooling rules were scored against exact move values: plain mean, confidence weighting, trust weighting, a bottom-tail trust gate, and pruning the 4 least-trusted of 12 rollouts and replacing them with 4 normal ones. Pre-registered (PREREG-R7-E3.md), 3 seeds, one L4, independent audit.
page.result: Gate passed, reproducing round 6 exactly (16 rollouts cut a 4-move-old belief's KL by 48.2%). Keys: pure salience K3 reached a gap of 0.234 [0.215, 0.254], failing the 0.28 bar; K3c reached 0.661 [0.642, 0.679]. With K3c keys, attention pooling's belief divergence between left- and right-preferring search was 10.8x below scaled mixing and 10.2x below Ataraxos-style pooling, and its KL to the exact posterior was lower than every baseline's, so E3-D1 passed. Trust ranking passed all four bars: Spearman with rollout accuracy +0.347 overall and +0.369 within a move's 16 rollouts, against -0.395 and -0.551 for confidence. Trust pooling failed: every trust rule beat confidence weighting by about 63%, but none beat the plain mean (MSE 0.01366): trust gate 0.01394, trust weighting 0.01412, prune-and-replace 0.01431 (significantly worse).
page.sowhat: Two things the spec assumed did not hold here. The key gap came from centring, not from salience: in a bag that leans 85/15 one way, centring makes the minority flank's keys point away from the majority's, and the pooling rules barely changed between K3 and K3c. And the exploratory rollouts as built here (tempered draws plus one type swap) were not hallucination traps: they were about as accurate as normal ones and less often overconfident, so a trust head trained on real outcomes rightly trusted them about as much. Trust does single out the worst individual rollouts, but most of the pooled error is bias that every rollout shares, which no weighting or pruning can remove; dropping rollouts only adds noise.
page.decided: Recorded the gate and E3-D1 as passed and E3-D2 as failed, as pre-registered; post hoc diagnostics are labelled and change no verdict. Not run or chosen: an exploratory tier that is actually unreliable; using trust to choose which moves to search rather than how to pool; key tests on unskewed bags, where centring cannot create a gap.

experiments.title: Round 7 E1: Jacobi-Richardson and weight-tied attention pools, key attribution and coverage-complete PUCT (6x6 ShipHunt)

page.why: Round 6 left three open points: its looped linear pool's normalisation cancelled deduplication; attn_L3's margin over kc_dedup might have come from its keys rather than from attention; and key-space PUCT stopped at 94.9% coverage. Gemini's round-7 spec tests a fix for each, and asks that the world model be saved so that no later round retrains it.
page.what: The round-5/6 6x6 board with a dense sonar field; the 669k-parameter world model retrained once more and saved per seed. Pools trained to the model's own reference: attn_L3 with raw, salience and combined keys; a weight-tied attention pool (one block applied 3 times); an exact Jacobi-Richardson normal-equation pool (812 parameters); kc_dedup with raw and with salience keys; a one-step precision-crowding pool. Three protocols: both searches read the 6 tiles that cover the board; active key-space PUCT under mixed and clean reads; same-patch bags at three noise levels. 3 seeds, pre-registered, exact Bayes for scoring only.
page.result: The weight-tied pool shows no detectable difference from attn_L3 with 3 seeds (KL 0.0317 vs 0.0328, JSD 0.0066 vs 0.0069) at 37% of the parameters. The Jacobi pool (KL 0.041) beats the round-6 linear pool (0.068) and adds support as noise grows (W(8)/W(1) 1.40, 1.82, 2.20 across the three noise levels), but 16 identical clean reads weigh 1.45x one (bar 1.25). PUCT covers 98.6% of cells vs 83.0% open loop; attn_L3's policy dependence falls 2.9x with mixed reads and 5.4x with clean reads, and KL falls 51-53%. Swapping kc_dedup's keys from raw to salience closes 44-80% of its gap to attn_L3, but swapping attn_L3's own keys closes only 5-9%, so the gap does not split into a key share and a pool share; attn_L3 still beats salience-key kc_dedup by 5-7.5%, and its high-noise margin over raw-key kc_dedup is 14.8% (bar 20%).
page.sowhat: No cost of weight tying was detectable with 3 seeds, so a looped one-block pool is a candidate cheap stand-in for attn_L3. Salience keys matter far more for a one-step crowding pool than for attention. With coverage-complete search, evidence one search never saw is no longer the main source of policy dependence; read noise and the pool's response to which reads each search made are (interpretation).
page.decided: Recorded E1-D0, E1-D1.1, E1-D2.1 and E1-D2.2 as passed, and E1-D1.2 (the Jacobi pool's clean deduplication, 1.45 vs bar 1.25) and E1-D3 (the MSE margin over raw-key kc_dedup at high noise, 14.8% vs 20%) as failed, so E1-D1 and E1-D3 fail. Saved theta_real v2 for each seed in li-net/r7e1/ckpt/. Not run, for gemini's next round: a Jacobi pool with its ridge tied to read precision; a PUCT ablation that splits the score change from the key change; a policy-independence test with matched read multiplicity.

page.why: In [Round 6 E2](exp-r6-e2-sudoku-local.html), failed rollouts went wrong at the first guess, about step 3 of 60, and never recovered. So gemini’s round-7 spec branched at the first few guesses instead of rolling out flat.
page.what: Same three 2.7M-parameter nets and sudoku-extreme boards, no retraining. The beam fills forced cells greedily, branches at each stall into every plausible digit, keeps the 16 most probable boards per level for 2-4 levels, then finishes them with rollouts, at no more passes than 16 flat rollouts. We compared it with flat rollouts, a one-stall Landmark and greedy forced steps. Pre-registered and hashed before scoring.

page.sowhat: The first guess is no longer the main loss: the beam keeps the solution path on 71-91% of boards. The rollouts below the last level then lose it, and deeper beams were worse (post hoc). Greedy forced steps hurt by 3 points.

experiments.title: Round 8 E-MS-SAFE-ANCHOR: 6x6 Stratego search anchored at the current-turn belief, corner worlds vs corrupted rollouts

page.why: Rounds 6 and 7 started 6x6 Stratego search from a 4-move-old belief (KL 0.185) and never gave it the net's own current belief (0.047). Gemini's round-8 spec asked two of Kelvin's questions. Can search start from the strong current belief and never make it worse as rollouts are added (K = 0 to 16)? And can a trust head tell legitimate but surprising 'corner worlds' from rollouts that are simply corrupted, so that weighting by window consistency and trust beats the plain mean? It reused round 5's trained networks, so nothing was retrained.
page.what: Beliefs: every pooling rule starts from the net's current belief and adds rollout evidence; rollouts are skewed 85/15 toward one flank and pooled in nested bags of 1 to 16. Naive rules (raw determinization counts; a fixed-step Ataraxos-style rule) are compared with fitted ones (scaled mixing, key deduplication, a 3-layer attention pool and a weight-tied looped attention pool), fitted on calibration positions against the true hidden pieces. Action values: per legal move, 16 clean rollouts whose hidden pieces are drawn from the 4-move-old belief and weighted by how well they explain the opponent's last moves, plus 6 corrupted ones (all sampled pieces changed; half one-move-deep, half random playouts). A trust head, trained on real game results, never sees which rollouts were corrupted. Pre-registered (PREREG-R8-E3.md), 3 seeds, one L4, independent audit, plus one labelled post hoc rerun.
page.result: Naive rules wrecked the anchor: raw counts took KL from 0.049 to 0.640 at 16 rollouts, the fixed-step rule to 4.78. The fitted one-parameter scaled mixing never hurt and reached 0.046. The attention pools, as registered, degraded the anchor to 0.635 and 0.585: their calibration loss fell from 1.12 to 0.98, a sign that they memorised the calibration positions. Rerun post hoc with early stopping on held-out calibration positions, both kept their initial small step in every seed: safe (KL 0.0463 at 16) but no better than scaled mixing. Values: window-consistency weighting did not lower MSE (0.0141 vs 0.0139 for the plain mean); its slightly lower bias was within noise. The trust head ranked rollout errors at +0.33, below the 0.40 bar, and trust gating (0.0153) lost to the plain mean (0.0143).
page.sowhat: A strong current belief was easy to protect here: the rules with a small fitted step stayed below it at every rollout count and gained a few percent. Nothing here found a learned rule that does better than that; the attention pools either memorised their training positions or, held back by early stopping, stayed at their initial small step. The corner-world question did not get a fair test: corrupting every sampled piece barely hurt one-move-deep rollouts, and two opponent moves are too little evidence to weight worlds by. A real test needs rollouts that are clearly worse and more window evidence.
page.decided: Recorded E3-D1 and E3-D2 as failed, as pre-registered; the early-stopping rerun is labelled post hoc and changes no verdict. Not run or chosen: aggregators fitted on many more calibration positions or against a smoothed target; a noisy tier with a verified large error; longer windows for consistency weighting.

experiments.title: Round 8 E1: anytime safety with an anchor token, a precision-aware Jacobi ridge and the PUCT attribution (6x6 ShipHunt)

page.why: Kelvin asked whether search can ever make a belief worse than where it started as more reads arrive. Round 7 also left three loose ends: a Jacobi pool that did not deduplicate identical clean reads, an econ_kc pool fitted on the wrong bags, and a PUCT coverage gain that changed keys and score together.
page.what: Round 7's saved world model, loaded unchanged in each seed. The root belief enters the attention pools as an anchor token with zero shift and a precision that grows with the root's anchor readings, and crowding is weighted by precision. Pools are trained on the model's own reference over roots of 2, 6, 12 and 18 anchor readings and 0 to 32 reads. Tests: an anytime curve from the standard root on an interleaved 32-read stream; curves from 6-, 12- and 18-anchor roots with 90/10 skewed noisy reads; controlled same-patch bags at three noise levels; a 2x2 PUCT factorial. 3 seeds, pre-registered, exact Bayes for scoring only.
page.result: The weight-tied attention pool's KL fell at every step in every seed, from 0.280 to 0.030 after 32 reads on the standard root, and below every stronger root at every K (by at least 0.023 from the 18-anchor root with tau 0.3/1.5 reads), in mean test KL over 500 boards. ataraxos_mmd, scaled_mix and R6's 4-step linear pool turn back up after 16 to 24 reads. The 18-anchor root sits at KL 0.144, and mmd still improves it at K = 16, so the rule's premise of a root that naive pools degrade did not hold. jacobi_lin_T4 with a precision-aware ridge deduplicates clean reads (W(16)/W(1) 1.16) and adds support for noisy ones (2.82), with KL 0.041 against a 0.040 bar. econ_kc fitted on mixed-tier probes still over-weights clean duplicates (1.42). PUCT coverage: 0.920 (raw keys, R6 score), 0.958 (raw keys, R7 score), 0.965 (salience keys, R6 score), 0.988 (salience keys, R7 score).
page.sowhat: In this testbed, attention pools that see the root as an anchor token were anytime-safe in mean test KL: on the five tested curves, more reads never left the belief worse than the root. Pools without the anchor token were not. Testing the degradation premise needs a much stronger root than 18 of 36 readings.

page.why: In [Round 7 E2](exp-r7-e2-sudoku-beam.html) the beam kept the solution path on most boards, but the rollouts below it left a quarter of the budget unused and its first rollout per branch was greedy. Gemini's round-8 spec fixed all three, and asked whether more search budget ever makes beliefs worse.
page.what: Same three nets, boards and beam, no retraining. Below the beam, every branch gets a fully random rollout in turn until 99.5% of the passes are spent. We then ran the same search at 1 to 32 rollouts' worth of passes. Pre-registered and hashed before scoring; baselines from Round 7.
page.result: The full-budget beam finds the answer on 42.8% of boards: above flat rollouts (40.2%), not above Round 7's starved beam (44.5%).
page.sowhat: Spending the whole budget did not help, so the loss below the beam is not unused passes. With check-gated pooling, more budget lowered KL at every step in every seed, but on unsolved boards it stays safe only when the net's own check is reliable (not seed 103).
page.decided: Recorded the budget and monotonicity rules as passed and the witness, KL and unresolved-board rules as failed. A post-hoc rerun showed a flagged gap between sibling runs was sampling noise, and that keeping one greedy rollout per branch helps: 46.7% of boards, +2.3 points over Round 7's beam (CI crosses 0).

experiments.title: Round 9 E2: the hybrid full-budget landmark beam and the self-consistent leaf check (sudoku-extreme)

page.why: In [Round 8 E2](exp-r8-e2-sudoku-anytime.html) spending the whole budget below the beam did not beat Round 7's starved beam, and unsolved boards were safe only when the net's own check was reliable (not seed 103). Gemini's round-9 spec asked which completion change matters, and whether a check that reads the finished board can make unsolved boards safe on every seed.
page.what: Same three nets, boards and beam, no retraining. Below the beam, four ways to finish each branch at the same full budget: Round 7's beam, all-random rollouts (R8), plus one greedy rollout per branch, plus greedy forced steps (P8_hybrid). Leaves are pooled only if the net's check, its confidence while filling, and its own re-read of the finished board all agree. Pre-registered and hashed before scoring; one process at a time on the GPU.
page.result: P8_hybrid finds the answer on 45.2% of boards, level with Round 7's beam. With the leaf self-check, unsolved boards return the one-pass belief exactly in every seed, and seed 103's false accepts fall from 9.6% to 0%.
page.sowhat: The greedy rollout is the active ingredient, and none of the completion changes is significantly better than random rollouts over 3 seeds. The self-check's safety is real on seed 103, the only seed with false accepts, but the gate passes only greedy completions, so extra budget past 16 rollouts adds no new accepted leaves.
page.decided: Recorded the budget, monotonicity and unresolved-safety rules as passed and the witness and KL rules as failed. The audit found that the gate's confidence-while-filling test only lets greedy completions through; a gate on the board re-read alone is the next candidate (proposed, not run).

Seeds 101 and 102 had no invalid accepted leaves to reject; seed 103 had 323 (about 30 distinct completions), all rejected by the board re-read (AUROC 0.99998), while the confidence-while-filling q does not separate them (AUROC 0.35).
Prefix vs independent in one process: 44.5% vs 45.2% (13 vs 24 discordant boards, p = 0.10), so no Round 8-style anomaly.

experiments.title: Round 9 E1: anytime safety from a genuinely strong root, and a precision-aware 1-step crowding pool (6x6 ShipHunt)

page.why: Round 8 could not test Kelvin's question from a strong root: its 18-anchor root sat at KL 0.144 and even the naive pools improved it. Round 9 builds a root from 30-34 of the 36 readings and asks whether adding reads can leave the belief worse than that root, and whether a 1-step crowding pool with a precision-dependent ridge gets the three-regime weight law.
page.what: Round 7's saved world model, loaded unchanged in each seed. The strong root (32 of 36 readings, chosen on calibration boards) gets 24 reads in two ways: cumulative-context reads on the root's evidence, as in round 8, and bounded reads on just the 2 standard anchors plus a patch, whose shifts are added to the strong root. The anchor-aware attention pools are trained on both kinds of bags over 7 root strengths. econ_prec_K3 gives the 1-step pool a ridge softplus(a - b beta); jacobi_lin_T4_prec gets a three-term loss. 3 seeds, pre-registered, exact Bayes for scoring only.
page.result: With bounded reads, every pool without the anchor token ended above the strong root by 24 reads: mix at once (+0.21), the learned pools jacobi_lin_T4_prec, econ_prec_K3 and kc_dedup from the first read, and ataraxos_mmd, scaled_mix and the 4-step looped_lin_T4 from 4 reads on. The anchor-aware pools stayed just below the root (-0.003 at 16 reads, 3-seed mean). With cumulative-context reads every pool except kc_K1 stayed below the root, and the anchor pools gained 0.017. jacobi_lin_T4_prec dedups clean reads (1.11), adds support for noisy ones (2.52) and reaches KL 0.035; econ_prec_K3 reaches 1.267 on clean reads against a 1.25 bar.
page.sowhat: In this testbed, adding bounded reads to a strong root made the belief worse for every pool that lacks the anchor token. Pools that see the root as an anchor token avoided this here, but they gained little, and they were trained on such bags. At the strongest root (34 readings) they hovered within 0.0007 of it, and the safety rule would fail there; the PASS rests on the reading that selected 32, which gemini approved before launch.
page.decided: Recorded E1-D0, E1-D1.1, E1-D1.2 (on approved reading 1) and E1-D2.2 as passed and E1-D2.1 as failed (econ_prec_K3 clean W(16)/W(1) 1.267 vs 1.25; its D3 MSE not distinguishable from econ_kc_K3's). Not run, for gemini's next round: the anchor pools trained on cumulative-context bags only (an ablation of the training bags); the anchor token's crowding term added to the 1-step and Jacobi pools.
